issues.title: A visa is required almost everywhere
issues.category_name: Visas, permits and the right to arrive
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: The Iranian passport gives visa-free or visa-on-arrival access to roughly 40 destinations and none of them are the countries people actually emigrate to. Every move starts from a standing refusal.

details.description: Henley Passport Index 2026: Iran ranked 90th, visa-free or visa-on-arrival to 40 destinations. Other indices rank it as low as 190th depending on whether eVisa and visa-on-arrival are counted.
details.notes: Indices disagree because they count different things. Henley is the usual citation; state the index when quoting a rank.

details.description: Iranian passport holders cannot enter the UAE, Libya, Syria or the United States on the passport alone - the UAE exclusion matters most in practice because Dubai is a common transit and visa-interview hub.
Because nothing is visa-free, every trip - including a trip taken only to attend another country's visa interview - needs its own application, fee, biometrics appointment and travel.
details.money_note: Compounding: each leg is a separate fee.
details.time_note: Per application, in parallel where allowed.

details.description: Conference attendance, client meetings, on-site interviews and family events are all gated. The professional cost is invisible on paper: the invitations stop coming once a person is known to be hard to move.
details.notes: Frequently described in diaspora accounts; not quantified here.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the conference Omid cannot attend
details.description: Omid's paper is accepted at a conference in Lisbon in May. The Schengen application needs an appointment in Yerevan, three months' bank statements he cannot produce, and eight weeks he does not have. He withdraws the paper and his supervisor presents it. His name stays on it; his face is not in the room.
details.energy_note: Published, and absent from your own work.

issues.title: No US consular services inside Iran since 1980
issues.category_name: Visas, permits and the right to arrive
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: The US embassy in Tehran has not issued visas since 1980, so every US visa application requires international travel to a third country before the process even begins.

details.description: Applicants are routed to Ankara, Istanbul, Dubai, Abu Dhabi or Yerevan. Reporting suggests Ankara handles roughly 60% of Iranian J-1 cases with Abu Dhabi taking most of the rest.
details.notes: Consultancy page; share figures unofficial.

details.aspect: The interview trip itself needs a visa
details.description: Turkey is visa-free for Iranians, which is why Ankara and Istanbul carry the volume. Armenia is visa-free. The UAE is not - a Dubai or Abu Dhabi interview requires a UAE visa first, an application that is itself frequently refused for young Iranian men.
details.notes: The UAE refusal pattern for young single Iranian men is widely reported in forums; no official statistic located.

details.aspect: Direct cost of a single interview trip
details.description: Flights and accommodation for one interview trip estimated at USD 800-1,500 on top of the USD 185 visa fee and, for students, the USD 220 SEVIS fee.
details.money_note: One trip, no repeat visit.

details.aspect: Repeat trips when documents are requested
details.description: Administrative processing often asks for further documents or a second interview, and the applicant has usually returned to Iran by then. Each round trip repeats the full cost.
details.money_note: Per additional trip.

details.description: Applicants who moved to Turkey or Armenia to be near a post must maintain legal residence there for months or years while the case sits. Residence permit refusal or expiry can collapse the whole application.
details.money_note: Rent and permit costs while waiting.
details.notes: Common pattern in Iranian applicant forums; deserves layer-5 research against real case accounts.

details.description: Omid flies Tehran-Yerevan for his interview: USD 320 return, three nights at USD 55. The officer takes his passport and issues a 221(g). Eleven weeks later the consulate emails asking for his military service card and a CV. He flies back to hand in two sheets of paper. Total for the second trip: USD 430. He has now spent more on travel than the visa fee, twice.
details.money_note: Two return trips plus accommodation.
details.energy_note: Flying to another country to deliver a photocopy.

issues.title: US travel bans: restriction, lifting, reinstatement
issues.category_name: Visas, permits and the right to arrive
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.era_note: Restricted 2017-2021; open 2021-2025; restricted again from June 2025; full suspension from 1 Jan 2026.
issues.summary: Iran has been under some form of US entry restriction for most of the period since 2017. As of 1 January 2026 Iranian nationals face a complete suspension of both immigrant and non-immigrant visas.

details.description: 27 Jan 2017. Suspended entry from Iran and six other Muslim-majority countries for 90 days. Over 700 travellers detained; up to 60,000 visas provisionally revoked, including already-issued ones.
details.time_note: Nominal suspension period; practical effect longer.
details.energy_note: Revocation of an already-granted visa mid-journey.

details.description: 24 Sep 2017. Suspended immigrant and most non-immigrant visas for Iranians, explicitly exempting F-1, M-1 and J-1 students. Upheld by the Supreme Court in Trump v. Hawaii, 585 U.S. 667 (2018).

details.aspect: The waiver that was not a waiver
details.description: PP 9645 provided for case-by-case waivers. Through March 2019 the State Department reported 440 waivers granted to Iranian nationals - 279 non-immigrant and 161 immigrant - out of roughly 33,900 Iranian applicants subject to the ban. Under 2%.
details.time_note: Waiver adjudication ran for months to years with no status.
details.energy_note: A process that exists on paper and almost never resolves.
details.source_name: US State Department waiver figures via NIAC

details.description: 20 Jan 2021. Biden ended PP 9645 and PP 9983 restrictions. Iranian restrictions lifted immediately, though COVID-era post closures meant practical resumption was slower.

EO 14161 (20 Jan 2025) ordered enhanced vetting and a 60-day review. Restrictions took effect June 2025. The proclamation of 16 Dec 2025, effective 1 Jan 2026, placed Iran among 19 countries under complete suspension of immigrant and non-immigrant visas. There is no separate waiver application - an applicant must apply and argue the case at interview.
details.energy_note: Plans built during the open window collapsed.

details.description: The four-year open window (2021-2025) drew people into multi-year plans - university offers, job offers, family petitions - that the December 2025 proclamation stranded. The cost is not the ban alone but the sunk investment made in reliance on its absence.
details.money_note: Sunk application, tuition deposit, relocation and legal spend.

details.description: Implementation of EO 13769 caught people already travelling: over 700 travellers were detained and up to 60,000 visas were provisionally revoked, including visas already issued and in passports.
details.energy_note: Lawful on departure, unlawful on arrival.

details.description: Through March 2019 the State Department reported 440 waivers granted to Iranian nationals against roughly 33,900 applicants subject to the ban - 279 non-immigrant and 161 immigrant.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the offer that expired in the gap
details.description: Reza is admitted to a PhD at Georgia Tech starting September 2026 with a funded position. On 16 December 2025 the proclamation lands. The department holds the place until March, then gives it to the next candidate. The USD 2,400 he spent on applications, tests and transcripts is not refundable and the funding line is gone.
details.energy_note: A future cancelled by a document you were not consulted about.

issues.title: Refusal rates far above average
issues.category_name: Visas, permits and the right to arrive
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Where Iranians can apply, they are refused more often. Elevated refusal is priced into every plan: applications are made in duplicate, and refusal itself becomes evidence against the next application.

details.description: Iran's Schengen refusal rate was 26.33% in 2024 (42,653 refusals), down from 30.3% in 2023, against a Schengen-wide average of about 14.6%. Sweden refused 51.57% of Iranian applicants; France refused the most in absolute terms, 10,051 of 39,146.
details.money_note: Schengen fee is not refunded on refusal.

details.description: Iran's FY2023 adjusted refusal rate for B visitor visas was 53.26% - among the highest in the world, alongside Pakistan.
details.source_name: US Dept of State FY23 adjusted refusal rates

details.description: Most application forms ask whether a visa has ever been refused by any country. A single refusal must then be declared for life, and is weighed against the applicant everywhere else.
details.energy_note: A permanent mark generated by a discretionary decision with no reasons.
details.notes: Standard question on UK, Canadian, Australian and US forms.

details.aspect: No appeal on most visitor refusals
details.description: UK visitor refusals carry no right of appeal and no administrative review; Schengen refusals have an appeal route that differs by member state and is rarely used successfully from Iran.

Refusal reasoning commonly turns on 'ties to home country' - property, dependants, stable employment. A young, single, childless man scores worst on every limb of that test, which is a gendered outcome produced by a facially neutral rule.
details.notes: Mechanism is documented in visa guidance generally; per-nationality gender breakdowns are not published. Layer-5 target.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - Sweden refused more than half
details.description: Sweden refused 51.57% of Iranian Schengen applicants in 2024 while Switzerland approved 90.25%. The same applicant, the same file, a different consulate - and opposite odds.
details.energy_note: Outcome determined by which flag is on the building.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the money kept on refusal
details.description: Schengen states refused 42,653 Iranian applications in 2024. At EUR 90 each, roughly EUR 3.8 million in non-refundable fees was collected from refused Iranian applicants in a single year.
details.money_note: Per application, not refunded.
details.energy_note: Refusal as a revenue line.
details.notes: Arithmetic mine: 42,653 x EUR 90.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the refusal he must declare forever
details.description: Maryam is refused a Schengen visa in 2019 for 'intention to leave the territory could not be ascertained'. In 2024 she applies to Canada. Question 2(b): have you ever been refused a visa by any country? She answers yes, attaches an explanation, and spends four months in additional review because of a five-year-old refusal that came with no reasons she could rebut.
details.energy_note: One unexplained no, declared for the rest of your life.

issues.title: Administrative processing and 221(g) holds
issues.category_name: Visas, permits and the right to arrive
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: A consular officer who cannot decide issues a 221(g) and puts the case into administrative processing. For Iranian applicants, especially in STEM, this is close to routine and has no deadline.

details.description: INA 221(g). Government processing time for these cases is indefinite. Most resolve in months; some take years; some never resolve.
details.time_note: Reported range from months to over two years.

details.description: Applicants in technology, engineering and science fields are routed into Visas Mantis security checks. Iranian STEM applicants are among the most affected groups.
details.notes: Mantis exists to screen against the Technology Alert List.

details.aspect: No status, no escalation, no clock
details.description: State will not accept a status inquiry until 60 days after processing begins. Because it is framed as a national security matter, universities and members of Congress cannot influence speed or outcome, and once started it cannot be withdrawn.
details.energy_note: Total loss of agency: nothing the applicant does changes anything.

details.description: A writ of mandamus in US federal court can compel the consulate to act - not to approve. Legal fees are the cost of getting a decision at all.
details.money_note: Typical US mandamus legal fees.
details.notes: Fee band from immigration firm marketing; verify before citing.

details.description: Because the interview happened abroad, the passport is often held by the post. The applicant cannot travel onward or, sometimes, home, while the hold runs.
details.money_note: Extended stay abroad with no work rights.
details.notes: Recurrent in applicant forums; layer-5 target for specific accounts.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - 45% of Iranian cases, 60-120 days added
details.description: One estimate puts 221(g) administrative processing as affecting roughly 45% of Iranian applicants and adding 60-120 days, against a median of about 210 days from DS-160 to issuance and interview waits of 60-180 days.
details.notes: Consultancy estimate, not State Department data.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - choosing a post as strategy
details.description: Consultancies advise that post choice matters: Dubai officers are described as used to Iranian applicants with diversified business interests and substantial portfolios, while Ankara and Yerevan see fewer Iranian cases - more individual attention, less pattern recognition for borderline files.
details.energy_note: Gaming the geography of who judges you.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - fourteen months, then the job was gone
details.description: Omid's H-1B interview is in Dubai in March. Administrative processing begins. He may not enquire for 60 days. At month nine the employer asks whether he can start; at month eleven they withdraw the offer; at month fourteen the visa is issued. He now holds a valid work visa and no job to use it for.
details.energy_note: Approved, on the day it stopped mattering.

issues.title: Canada screened Iranians by nationality, age and sex
issues.category_name: Security screening, vetting and intelligence referral
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Iranian nationality and being male
issues.era_note: Mandatory indicators abandoned August 2018; referral volumes stayed high.
issues.summary: Before August 2018 Canada used a mandatory screening indicator for Iranian applications built on nationality combined with age and sex alone. Matching applicants were automatically referred to CBSA and CSIS. This is the single clearest documented instance of an Iranian man being screened for being an Iranian man.

details.description: NSIRA found that prior to reforms in August 2018, a mandatory CBSA-developed indicator used by IRCC for Iranian applications was based entirely on Iranian nationality combined only with age and sex. Applicants matching it were automatically referred to CBSA and CSIS.
details.energy_note: Screening triggered by demographic category, not by conduct.
details.notes: This is the strongest single citation in the whole dataset for the 'Iranian + male' intersection. Read the full summary before relying on it.

details.description: The government abandoned mandatory indicators in 2018 over concerns about efficacy and the delays they caused - not, on the record, over discrimination.
NSIRA noted IRCC did not record which indicator triggered a referral. An applicant therefore cannot establish why they were screened, which forecloses most avenues of challenge.
details.energy_note: Unprovable by design.

issues.title: Volume and duration of Canadian security screening
issues.category_name: Security screening, vetting and intelligence referral
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Referral to security screening rarely produces a refusal. It produces years of silence. The harm is the delay, and the delay is the part nobody is accountable for.

details.description: IRCC data released under the Access to Information Act shows 47,635 applications from Iranian nationals referred to security screening between January 2019 and 31 July 2025.
details.source_name: IRCC ATIP data, via GoFar Global analysis
details.notes: Underlying figure is IRCC ATIP; the analysis is third-party. Request the ATIP package directly if this is going into a filing.

details.aspect: Almost nobody is actually found inadmissible
details.description: In 2023, 6,585 Iranian temporary-residence applicants were referred and 10 came back non-favourable - about 0.15%. Referral is triggered by category, such as military service or a sensitive field of study, not by individual suspicion.
details.energy_note: Years lost to a process that clears 99.85% of those it delays.
details.notes: Ratio is the most useful single fact here: the process is not filtering, it is queuing.

details.description: CSIS received 538,100 immigration and citizenship screening requests in 2024, up from 493,000 in 2023 and about 300,000 annually in the preceding five years. In 2024, 87.5% of CSIS security clearance assessments were for citizenship applicants or asylum claimants.

details.aspect: What it looks like from inside
details.description: The file shows 'In Progress' under Background Verification for months or years with no update. Referral is usually only visible by ordering GCMS notes; it is never announced.
details.money_note: GCMS notes request fee and/or consultant fee.

details.description: Withdrawing and re-applying resets processing time and almost certainly triggers the same check, so the one obvious self-help move is a trap.
Where the wait exceeds what is reasonable, a Federal Court mandamus application can compel a decision. It is the standard advice, which tells you how routine the problem is.
details.money_note: Canadian Federal Court mandamus fees.

details.description: Petitions before the House of Commons assert that in 2024 Iranian applicants were referred at a rate far exceeding applicants from other countries, with delays far beyond published standards and no transparency about the criteria for 'comprehensive' screening. One petition specifically concerns Iranians holding Canadian Master's and PhD degrees nominated under the PNP.
details.notes: A petition is an assertion by petitioners, not a government finding. Cite it as what it is.

details.aspect: Degrees do not help; they may hurt
details.description: The PNP petition describes people with Canadian graduate degrees being held. Advanced study in a technical field is itself a referral trigger, so the usual advice - get more qualified - makes the delay more likely.
details.notes: Inference from the referral-by-category finding plus the petition's population. Layer-5 target: get the ATIP breakdown by field of study.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - ten years in background check
details.description: Vice reported Iranian students whose applications stalled up to ten years against a published six-month estimate, missing job opportunities, conferences and family weddings while their lives were held open.
details.time_note: Six-month estimate against a ten-year reality.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - a Canada Research Chair waiting
details.description: The Toronto Star reported a Canada Research Chair at the University of Ottawa who waited a year for security clearance and could not apply for PR without it.
details.notes: Seniority is no protection - arguably the opposite.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - eleven US visas, still singled out
details.description: One applicant described feeling 'singled out' despite having been granted eleven US visas and passing three prior Canadian background checks.
details.energy_note: A clean record across fourteen prior checks counts for nothing.

details.description: CBC reported a group of 55 couples who found each other through social media over similar stuck applications - years-long PR waits combined with refused visitor visas keeping partners in different countries.
details.energy_note: Separation enforced from both directions at once.

details.description: Roughly one in six security screening referrals in Canada involves an Iranian applicant - a share far above Iran's share of applications.
details.notes: This is the defensible version of the 'most Iranian applications go to intelligence' claim. Use this, not a 95% figure.

details.description: On the CanadaVisa 'PR applicants from Iran' thread, posters report anything from six months to several years; one long-running estimate is one to three years for most Iranians. A common folk explanation - that Iran does not share applicant information with Canada - was contested in-thread as unsourced.
details.source_name: CanadaVisa forum - PR applicants from Iran
details.notes: Forum consensus, not data. Included because it shows what applicants believe, which drives their decisions.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the call centre cannot help
details.description: In a background-check thread a user stuck since January 2024 asked whether phoning helps. The practical answer: agents can read the status but cannot expedite or move anything.
details.energy_note: A helpline that confirms you are stuck.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the GCMS notes that explain nothing
details.description: Twenty-two months into a PR application showing 'In Progress', Nasrin pays CAD 40 for her brother's GCMS notes. The security screening section is four lines, three of them redacted. The visible line reads: referred for further assessment. That is the entire content of two years.
details.energy_note: Paying to read a redaction.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the promotion he could not accept
details.description: Omid is offered a team lead role in Vancouver conditional on PR. He is 26 months into background verification. He asks for a six-month extension, then another. The company promotes someone else and he stays on the work permit, doing the same job he did three years ago.
details.money_note: Foregone salary differential over three years.

issues.title: US security advisory opinions and the Technology Alert List
issues.category_name: Security screening, vetting and intelligence referral
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: The US equivalent: applicants whose field touches the Technology Alert List are referred for a Security Advisory Opinion. Iranian nationality plus a technical field is close to an automatic referral.

details.description: Visas Mantis SAOs screen applicants against the Technology Alert List, which covers nuclear, missile, aerospace, materials, sensors, information security and related fields.
Iranian applicants are concentrated in exactly the engineering and physical science disciplines the TAL covers, so the screen catches a large share of the population rather than a targeted subset.
details.notes: Directionally well supported; needs a field-of-study breakdown to state as fact. Layer-5 target.

details.aspect: Renewal risk for people already inside
details.description: A student or worker already in the US who leaves the country must re-apply abroad and can be caught in a new SAO, stranding them outside a life they have already built. The rational response is to stop leaving - which means not attending funerals, weddings or a parent's illness.
details.energy_note: Self-imposed exile from one's own family while lawfully resident.
details.notes: Extremely common account; layer-5 target for documented cases.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - a year of vetting, revoked in an afternoon
details.description: Shahab Dehghani's student visa was granted by the State Department after a year of intense vetting, and revoked by a CBP officer at the jetway. The two decisions used the same facts.
details.energy_note: One arm of government overruling another, at the door.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the lab he had to leave
details.description: Omid's PhD is in computational fluid dynamics. His advisor moves the group's work onto a project with a turbomachinery sponsor. Legal review flags the sponsor's export classification. Nobody says the word Iranian; he is simply moved to a different sub-project, on a different timeline, away from the part that publishes.
details.energy_note: Reassigned politely, out of the work that builds a career.

issues.title: Conscription is compulsory, and it gates the passport
issues.category_name: Military service and the male exit problem
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Iranian nationality and being male
issues.summary: Every Iranian man aged 18-49 owes 18-24 months of military service, and a man who has not served or been exempted generally cannot get a passport. The exit door is locked from the inside before any destination country is involved.

details.description: The Iranian constitution requires all men aged 18 to 49 to complete military service of 18 months to two years. Men who have not served generally cannot obtain a passport to leave the country.
details.time_note: Service length itself - 18 to 24 months of working life.
details.energy_note: Not a choice, and not deferrable indefinitely.

details.aspect: Education shortens it but does not remove it
details.description: Service is reduced by roughly 10 months for PhD holders, 8 for master's and 6 for bachelor's degrees.

details.aspect: The obligation follows the passport, not the address
details.description: Military liability attaches to Iranian citizenship, not residence. A man who has lived abroad for decades is still technically a conscript if he never served or obtained exemption - which makes any visit home a legal risk.
details.energy_note: No statute of limitations on the obligation; the risk never expires.

details.description: Conscription-liable men who have lived continuously abroad for at least three years can apply for an exit-facility stamp allowing two visits per Iranian year totalling 90 days. Overstaying the 90 days triggers a travel ban - the man cannot leave again.
details.energy_note: A visit home is a metered, revocable privilege.
details.source_name: Iranian Consulate Mumbai - exit facility for conscripts

details.aspect: Buying out - available, then not, then unclear
details.description: A buy-out scheme ran until around 2019 and was dropped for benefiting only the wealthy. In January 2022 a parliamentary budget committee floated exemptions at 250-600 million tomans (roughly USD 9,000-21,500), limited to absentees over 35 or those eight years past their due date, priced higher for the more educated. It was cancelled one day after being reported.
details.money_note: 2022 proposal only - withdrawn. Current rates differ.
details.energy_note: Policy that changes within 24 hours cannot be planned around.
details.notes: DO NOT cite the dollar band as a current price. It is a withdrawn proposal. Rates are set annually and move with the rial.

details.description: Men abroad for more than eight years can pay a fine and receive an exemption card, handled through an Iranian embassy or consulate without returning. The amount is set annually and tracks the rial, so it cannot be quoted in advance.
details.money_note: Highly variable; confirm with a consulate.

details.description: The cheapest legal exit - the absentee route - requires staying away eight years. A man who leaves at 20 cannot safely return until 28. That period covers most weddings, illnesses and deaths in a family.
details.energy_note: Chosen exile as the rational option.

details.description: Completed Iranian military service appears on the record and is reported as a category that triggers security referral in Canada. Serving creates the screening problem; not serving creates the passport problem. There is no option that avoids both.
details.energy_note: A double bind with no compliant path.
details.notes: The referral-by-category reporting names military service. This double bind is the core structural finding for Iranian men. Layer-5 target: find the IRCC indicator documentation naming service.

details.description: Canada listed the IRGC as a terrorist entity in June 2024. Conscripts assigned to IRGC-affiliated units - an assignment they did not choose - face arguments of inadmissibility for membership in a listed entity.
details.energy_note: Retroactive consequence for a posting assigned by lottery.
details.notes: Listing date is well documented; the inadmissibility consequence for conscripts is argued case by case. HIGH-VALUE layer-5 research target - find IRB decisions on conscript IRGC service.

details.description: The January 2022 buy-out scheme was reported on 30 January and cancelled on 31 January after public criticism that it sold exemptions to the rich. Families who began raising the money had one day.
details.energy_note: A plan with a one-day lifespan.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the arithmetic of going home
details.description: Omid left at 24 without serving. The absentee route requires eight years abroad; he can return in 2032, aged 32. His father will be 66. His mother has had two cardiac stents. He does the arithmetic once, writes it down, and never does it again.
details.energy_note: A number of years you can only bear to count once.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the card that arrives too late
details.description: Omid pays the absentee fine through the consulate in March. The exemption card is issued in Tehran in November and posted to his uncle. By the time it reaches him his father has died and been buried for five weeks.

See MIL-004. The IRB's Response to Information Request IRN201365.E and IRN104809.E establish that the service completion or exemption card is required for a passport, that refusal blocks a driver's licence and government employment, and that the exemption card states the reason for the exemption.
details.notes: ANSWERS MIL-001-008.

issues.title: Draft evasion as an asylum claim that is hard to win
issues.category_name: Military service and the male exit problem
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Iranian nationality and being male
issues.summary: Refusing conscription is a recognised basis for protection in principle, but proving it - and proving the punishment would be persecution rather than prosecution - is difficult and gendered.

details.description: Draft evasion alone is generally not persecution. Claims usually need conscientious objection, a disproportionate penalty, or a risk of being made to commit acts contrary to international law.
details.notes: General refugee-law principle; verify against destination-country case law.

details.description: The claimant is asked for evidence of a summons or penalty issued by the state he fled, obtainable only from that state.
details.energy_note: Asked to prove a case using documents only the persecutor holds.

details.description: Men without a gender-based or religious claim rely on political-opinion or conscientious-objection grounds, which turn heavily on the decision-maker's assessment of sincerity. Outcomes are consequently inconsistent.
details.notes: Widely asserted in practitioner commentary. NOT established here. Layer-5 target: grant-rate statistics by sex and claim type.

issues.title: Iran is outside the Apostille Convention
issues.category_name: Documents, translation, legalisation and proof
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Iran is not a party to the 1961 Hague Convention, so no Iranian document can be apostilled. Every document needs the long consular legalisation chain instead.

details.description: Iran is not a party to the Hague Convention of 5 October 1961. Legalisation for use in or from Iran must go through consular legalisation.
details.notes: Check whether Iran has acceded since this was written - accession would materially change this row.

details.description: Sworn translation, then Iranian Ministry of Justice, then Ministry of Foreign Affairs, then the destination country's embassy. Typically 10-20 working days per document type.
details.money_note: Per document set.

details.aspect: The Farsi original must stay attached
details.description: The translation must be certified and legalised together with the original, and the Farsi original must remain physically attached at every step. Separating them invalidates the chain.
details.energy_note: One clerical slip restarts the whole sequence.

details.description: A man who cannot return to Iran - conscription, political risk - cannot walk the chain himself. It must be done by a relative with power of attorney, which itself must be legalised through the same chain.
details.money_note: Agent or relative costs, courier, repeat fees.
details.energy_note: A recursive dependency on the country you left.

details.description: Incomplete files are placed on hold and kept open until the missing document arrives. A missing stamp produces indefinite limbo rather than a clean refusal that could be appealed.
details.energy_note: No decision to push back against.

details.description: Iranian export rules cap hand-woven carpet at 24 square metres per traveller, caviar at 125g and saffron at 150g - a reminder that what a family can carry out is itemised by the state down to the gram.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the power of attorney loop
details.description: Omid needs his birth certificate legalised. He cannot enter Iran. He must send his uncle a power of attorney - which must itself be notarised in Toronto, legalised by Global Affairs, then by the Iranian consulate, then couriered. Elapsed time before the actual task can begin: eleven weeks.
details.energy_note: Eleven weeks of queueing for permission to join a queue.

issues.title: Name transliteration inconsistency
issues.category_name: Documents, translation, legalisation and proof
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Persian names have no single Latin spelling. Passport, degree, bank record and visa can each carry a different transliteration, and every mismatch reads to an officer as a possible identity discrepancy.

details.description: Mohammad / Mohammed / Muhammad; Hosseini / Husseini / Hoseini. Different translators at different times produce different spellings of the same name.
Credential evaluators, banks and background-check firms match on name. A mismatch turns an automated check into a manual one, adding weeks.
details.money_note: Affidavits of one-and-the-same-person, re-translation.

details.description: Iranian identity documents foreground the father's name; many Western forms have no field for it, so it lands inconsistently in middle-name fields and propagates the mismatch.

issues.title: Police certificates that cannot be obtained
issues.category_name: Documents, translation, legalisation and proof
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Most immigration programs require a police clearance from every country lived in. Obtaining an Iranian certificate generally requires presence in Iran or a legalised power of attorney, and the result may still be questioned.

details.description: Canada, Australia and the UK all require police certificates covering every country of residence over a threshold period.

Iranian certificates are typically issued to the person in Iran or via a consulate with fingerprints and legalised authority. For a man who cannot return, the process depends entirely on consular cooperation.
details.energy_note: Dependence on the state you are seeking protection from.

details.description: Where the consulate accepts remote applications, fingerprints must be taken by an approved authority in the host country and couriered, adding cost and a failure point for rejected prints.

issues.title: Iranian credentials are slow and expensive to verify
issues.category_name: Education, credentials and academic recognition
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Credential evaluation is required for most skilled-migration and licensing routes. The Iranian chain has more steps than most, and verification depends on institutions that may not answer.

details.description: MSRT approval of academic documents; translation by a Ministry of Justice authorised translator with that ministry's certification; Ministry of Foreign Affairs validation of the MoJ stamp on translations attached to Farsi originals; then notarisation.

details.aspect: Sealed envelopes direct from the institution
details.description: WES requires documents sent directly by the institution in a sealed envelope, and may charge the applicant for the institution's verification fee.
details.money_note: Institutional verification fee, billed to the applicant.

details.description: Some Iranian medical and technical institutions verify only through internal portals requiring the applicant's own login and Persian navigation, so the evaluator cannot proceed without live cooperation from the applicant.
Direct outreach to Iranian universities gets inconsistent responses, better when made in Persian or on official letterhead. A non-responding registrar stalls the file with no route of appeal.
details.energy_note: Outcome depends on a stranger answering an email.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the login you must hand over
details.description: Some Iranian medical and technical institutions verify credentials only through internal portals requiring the applicant's own username and password, and Persian navigation - so the applicant must surrender personal credentials to an evaluator abroad, or do it live on a call.
details.energy_note: Hand over your password or lose the application.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - answered better in Persian, on letterhead
details.description: Evaluators report that Iranian universities respond more reliably when approached in Persian or on official letterhead - so the outcome partly depends on whether the foreign evaluator happens to employ a Persian speaker.
details.energy_note: Your file's fate resting on someone else's staffing.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the registrar who did not reply
details.description: WES emails Omid's university registrar in Tehran three times over four months. There is no reply. The file stays open, not refused. His Express Entry profile expires. Nobody at any point made a decision about him.
details.energy_note: Defeated by an unanswered email in another hemisphere.

issues.title: Sanctions and suspicion attach to Iranian universities
issues.category_name: Education, credentials and academic recognition
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Several Iranian universities carry export-control or sanctions designations. Graduates inherit the association, which affects admission, visa screening and employment even where the individual has no connection to the designated work.

details.description: Entity-list and sanctions designations attached to specific Iranian institutions cause automated flags on applications naming them.
details.notes: PLACEHOLDER - the specific designations and dates must be pulled from the BIS Entity List and EU/UK sanctions lists. Priority layer-5 target.

details.description: The flag follows the degree, not the person. An applicant who studied civil engineering at a designated university carries the same flag as one who studied something sensitive.
details.energy_note: A permanent mark acquired at 18 by choosing a university.

details.description: Some destination countries restrict Iranian nationals from nuclear, aerospace and certain materials programmes; the UK ATAS scheme screens postgraduate applicants in listed subjects and Iranian applicants are disproportionately refused.
details.notes: ATAS exists and is documented; the Iranian refusal rate assertion is NOT verified here. Layer-5 target - ATAS refusal statistics by nationality.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - designation is about the institution, not the graduate
details.description: See EDU-006 for the documented Sharif designations. The distinction that matters: entity listings bind transactions with the university, not the immigration status of people who studied there.
details.notes: EDU-002 was a placeholder in the first pass; EDU-006 now carries the verified detail.

issues.title: Ranking and recognition penalties
issues.category_name: Education, credentials and academic recognition
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Strong Iranian universities are under-represented in global rankings for reasons partly unrelated to teaching quality - sanctions on indexing and collaboration, limited international co-authorship, and language. Graduates are then assessed against the ranking.

details.description: Sharif, Tehran and Amirkabir are regarded regionally as strong engineering schools but rank below institutions their graduates outperform.
details.notes: UNVERIFIED as stated. Needs ranking data plus a defensible comparator. Layer-5 target.

details.description: Employers and admissions committees use ranking as a proxy. A graduate is discounted for an institutional position they did not cause and cannot change.

Points systems award for level of qualification rather than institution, so the ranking penalty bites at employment rather than at the visa - meaning it shows up after arrival, when it is hardest to absorb.

issues.title: Bank accounts closed abroad for nationality
issues.category_name: Banking, money movement and sanctions spillover
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Banks outside Iran have repeatedly closed or refused accounts for Iranian nationals who are lawfully resident and not covered by any sanction - over-compliance rather than legal requirement.

details.description: Deutsche Bank, Commerzbank and others suspended Iranian students' accounts and refused new applications, notifying customers of closure with no reason given. A Berlin Iranian refugee organisation reported complaints affecting hundreds.
details.energy_note: Closure letter with no reason and no appeal.

details.aspect: The German government said it was unlawful
details.description: Foreign Office official Emily Haber wrote to the institutions stating that blocking Iranian citizens' accounts had no legal basis, and called for a fresh audit of account management and new openings.
details.notes: Useful: the state itself characterised the practice as baseless. Strong material for a discrimination argument.

details.description: Commerzbank, Sparkasse and Comdirect were later reported refusing accounts to Iranian students, who described an 'unwritten rule' pushing them to close.

Advocacy reporting indicates as many as 15,000 accounts connected to people of Iranian heritage were restricted in an apparent sanctions-compliance effort, often without valid cause, despite US guidance that those not ordinarily resident in Iran need not be restricted.
details.notes: NIAC is an advocacy organisation; the figure is their submission, not a regulator's finding. Characterise it accurately.

details.description: Italian banks closed Iranian citizens' accounts in 2020, one customer told directly it was because of nationality. Malaysian banks conducted mass closures. HSBC discontinued accounts of customers from significantly sanctioned countries including Iran on internal risk assessment.

Losing the account means losing salary deposit, rent standing orders, utility direct debits, credit card and often the credit history attached to it. Rebuilding takes months and some of it does not come back.
details.money_note: Fees, missed payments, credit damage, re-establishment.
details.energy_note: Financial identity deleted without notice.

details.description: Proof of funds, settlement funds and sponsorship evidence all require bank statements. An applicant whose account was closed for being Iranian cannot produce the statements the immigration system demands.
details.energy_note: One arm of the state demands what another arm's policy destroyed.
details.notes: Strong structural point. Layer-5 target: find refusal decisions citing insufficient proof of funds where closure was the cause.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - told it was the nationality, out loud
details.description: An Italian bank customer was told directly that the account closure was because of her nationality; another concluded it was 'very likely' the cause after being given no explanation at all.
An affected academic described the banks' behaviour as being 'more Catholic than the Pope' - applying blanket nationality screening well beyond what sanctions law actually requires.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - thirty days' notice, no reason
details.description: Reza receives a letter from his German bank: the account will close in thirty days. No reason is given. His salary deposit, rent standing order, health insurance debit and two years of credit history are attached to it. He is a lawful resident on a Blue Card with a permanent employment contract.
details.energy_note: A letter that ends your financial existence in one paragraph.

issues.title: Money cannot move out of Iran through the banking system
issues.category_name: Banking, money movement and sanctions spillover
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Iran is disconnected from SWIFT for most purposes. Family savings, property proceeds and salary history cannot be transferred by any traceable route - which is exactly the route immigration systems require.

details.description: International transfers from Iranian banks to most destinations are unavailable, so value moves through sarafi (exchange house) and hawala networks.
Informal transfer carries a commission plus an exchange spread, commonly estimated at 2-8% of the amount, with no recourse if the counterparty fails.
details.money_note: Estimated 2-8% on a USD 25,000-100,000 transfer.
details.energy_note: Life savings moved on trust with no legal remedy.
details.notes: Percentage band is an estimate from general reporting. Layer-5 target: sarafi rate data.

details.description: Immigration proof-of-funds rules require a traceable origin and often six months of statements. Funds arriving by hawala have no paper trail, so money that exists cannot be shown to exist.
details.energy_note: Solvent on paper at home, destitute on paper abroad.

details.description: A large cash or informal-origin deposit by an Iranian national triggers AML review at the receiving bank - the same de-risking reflex that closes accounts.
details.notes: Feeds directly back into FIN-001.

details.aspect: Property that cannot be sold out
details.description: A family home in Tehran may be worth a deposit on a house abroad, but the proceeds cannot be moved. Wealth is effectively trapped inside the border.
details.money_note: Value stranded, not spent.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - six months of statements you cannot produce
details.description: Proof-of-funds rules typically want six months of statements showing a traceable origin. Money moved by sarafi arrives as a lump with no history, which reads to a visa officer exactly like money laundering.
details.energy_note: The only way to move it is the way that makes it unusable.

details.description: Canadian Express Entry requires proof of settlement funds scaled to family size. An applicant with a house in Tehran and no transferable currency fails a means test he would pass on any honest measure of wealth.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the proof of funds he cannot prove
details.description: Omid's family sells a Tehran apartment for the equivalent of USD 96,000. The money reaches Toronto in four transfers from three different names over five weeks, via a sarafi, at a 4.5% spread. IRCC asks for six months of statements showing the source. He has a lump sum from strangers and no document that explains it.
details.money_note: Spread and commission on USD 96,000.
details.energy_note: Solvent at home, unprovable abroad.

issues.title: Gold, crypto and stores of value
issues.category_name: Banking, money movement and sanctions spillover
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Blocked from ordinary banking, Iranians turn to gold and cryptocurrency - and are then blocked from those too, or treated as suspicious for using them.

details.description: Dealers applying sanctions screening decline Iranian-national customers or require documentation other customers do not.
details.notes: Reported anecdotally, matching the bank de-risking pattern. NOT verified. Layer-5 target.

details.aspect: Exchanges blocking by nationality and IP
details.description: Major crypto exchanges geo-block Iran and close accounts on detecting Iranian nationality, residence history or IP - including for users resident elsewhere.
details.energy_note: Assets frozen on an exchange with no appeal.
details.notes: Consistent with the documented GitHub/AWS/Slack pattern in TEC-001.

details.aspect: Using crypto becomes evidence against you
details.description: Having used crypto to move value out of Iran can itself attract AML scrutiny or sanctions questioning at the destination.

Iranian gold coins - the standard household savings instrument - are prohibited from export under any circumstances, while 150g of jewellery is allowed. The savings form that holds value is the one that cannot travel.

issues.title: Export control closes whole industries
issues.category_name: Work, licensing, export control and clearance
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Under the 'deemed export' rules, letting an Iranian national see controlled technical data counts as exporting to Iran. Because Iran is under arms embargo, the licence that would permit it is effectively unavailable - so defence, aerospace and parts of semiconductors simply do not hire.

details.description: 15 CFR 734.20: releasing technology or source code subject to the EAR to a foreign national is deemed an export to that person's country, even entirely inside the US. Visual inspection or conversation can count.

details.aspect: Why Iran is different from other foreign nationals
details.description: ITAR prohibits licences for countries under US and UN arms embargoes. Iran is in that category, so licensing is effectively unavailable rather than merely slow. Iran-specific sanctions reach further still, covering technical assistance to Iranian nationals ordinarily resident in Iran even when temporarily elsewhere.
details.energy_note: Not a queue - a closed door.

details.aspect: The green card is the escape hatch
details.description: The deemed export rule applies only to foreign persons. US citizens, lawful permanent residents, and protected individuals including refugees and asylees are US persons and are NOT subject to deemed-export licensing.
details.energy_note: Genuinely good news, and widely misunderstood by employers.
details.notes: IMPORTANT for the narrative and for real life: status, not ethnicity, controls here. Employers who refuse Iranian-born green card holders on export grounds are wrong in law.

details.description: Licences take months, cost money and are rarely pursued for one hire when citizen candidates exist. The practical result is a blanket practice of not hiring non-US persons for controlled roles.
details.energy_note: No refusal is ever stated in these terms; the application just does not progress.

details.description: DOJ's position is that employers must consider all work-qualified applicants and obtain authorisation where needed. Blanket 'US citizens only' postings can violate the INA. The law is therefore on the applicant's side and almost never invoked.
details.energy_note: A remedy that exists but nobody uses.
details.source_name: Littler - discrimination and deemed export laws
details.notes: Layer-5 target: DOJ IER settlements involving citizenship-status discrimination in export-controlled roles.

details.description: BIS licence conditions for 3E001/3E002 permit most silicon technology (bipolar, Bi-MOS, Bi-CMOS, CMOS) but not compound semiconductors such as gallium arsenide or silicon-on-sapphire. The boundary is granular, so whether a given job is closed depends on the exact process node and material.
Defence, aerospace and national-lab work are among the better-paid engineering tracks. Exclusion is not a delay but a permanent narrowing of the career surface, compounding over decades.
details.money_note: Illustrative cumulative differential, NOT a measured figure.

details.aspect: Security clearance is a separate, also-closed track
details.description: Clearance adjudication is distinct from export licensing. Foreign preference and foreign influence guidelines weigh family remaining in Iran, so even a naturalised citizen faces a harder adjudication because of who his parents are.
details.energy_note: Penalised for having a mother.
details.notes: Adjudicative Guidelines B and C are public. Layer-5 target: DOHA appeal decisions involving Iranian family ties - these are published and searchable, and would be strong specific material.

details.description: In ISCR Case No. 05-12088 the DOHA Appeal Board REVERSED a favourable decision. The judge had credited that the applicant resisted Iranian pressure to give up her US citizenship, that her father had no regime ties, and that she was US-born. The Board held an applicant with close family in a hostile country bears a 'heavy burden', and that close cases 'should be resolved in the favor of national security, rather than in the favor of the Applicant.'
details.energy_note: Winning at hearing and losing on appeal for having relatives.
details.notes: Verify the case number against the full text before citing - DOHA URLs are by FileId, not case number.

details.description: ISCR Case No. 04-09473: clearance denied where the applicant's grandmother, aunt, uncle and cousins were citizens and residents of Iran, compounded by foreign passport use.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - being persecuted counts against you
details.description: The pattern across decisions is that evidence the applicant's family had been TARGETED by the Iranian regime weighed AGAINST mitigation - because targeting establishes the regime's interest in them, and therefore the leverage.
details.energy_note: Victimhood as a security liability.
details.notes: The single most counter-intuitive finding in the dataset, and strong material.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - and it is not automatic
details.description: In one Guideline B/C appeal the Board expressly rejected the argument that denial is automatic, finding nothing suggesting a 'blanket' rule against applicants with close family in Iran - while still affirming the denial.
details.energy_note: Not a rule, just the outcome every time.

details.description: ISCR Case No. 07-00894 was GRANTED where the applicant had returned her passport to Iran, renounced Iranian citizenship, had no family, friends or financial interests in Iran, and all siblings and her mother lived in the US as citizens. The price of clearance was having nothing left in Iran at all.
details.energy_note: Clearance granted on proof of total severance.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the passport you cannot surrender
details.description: One denial turned on an applicant unwilling to surrender his Iranian passport because he needed it to settle his father's estate in Iran, while his eldest brother remained an Iranian citizen and resident.
details.energy_note: Choose: your father's estate, or your career.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the role that quietly closed
details.description: Omid interviews well for a turbine aerodynamics role and is told the team is excited. Two weeks later HR emails that the position has been put on hold. It is reposted a month later, same wording, with 'must be a US person' added to the requirements. Nobody has done anything unlawful and nobody has explained anything.
details.energy_note: The door closes without anyone being seen to close it.

details.description: See EMP-004. DOJ's Immigrant and Employee Rights section has penalised Clifford Chance (USD 132,000), Honda Aircraft (USD 44,626 plus monitoring), American CyberSystems and General Motors for exactly the exclusions described here.
details.energy_note: It is not just unfair. It has been found unlawful, repeatedly.
details.notes: ANSWERS EMP-001-005 - full detail in the new issue EMP-004.

issues.title: Licensed professions require re-qualification
issues.category_name: Work, licensing, export control and clearance
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by any immigrant regardless of origin
issues.summary: Doctors, nurses, engineers, lawyers and teachers cannot practise on a foreign credential. Re-qualification costs years and money, and for Iranians the verification step that underpins it is the fragile one.

details.description: Foreign-trained doctors typically face licensing examinations plus a residency place secured in competition with domestic graduates - commonly 3-7 years before independent practice.
Professional engineer designation requires credential assessment, examinations and supervised experience under a licensed engineer - which requires first getting hired without the designation.
Most people work outside their profession while re-qualifying. The income gap and skill decay during those years are the real cost, not the exam fees.
details.energy_note: Watching your profession recede while you drive to pay for the exam.

details.description: Maryam qualified in Tehran in 2019 and practised for four years. In Canada the pathway is an equivalency assessment, two written exams, a clinical exam and a qualifying year: roughly CAD 34,000 and three to five years. She drives for a delivery app in the evenings and studies in the afternoons.
details.energy_note: Your profession, visible through glass, for five years.

issues.title: Name-based hiring discrimination
issues.category_name: Work, licensing, export control and clearance
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Field experiments across several countries show identical CVs receive fewer callbacks under a Middle Eastern or Muslim-sounding name. The effect applies before any interview, so it is invisible to the person experiencing it.

details.description: Correspondence studies send matched CVs differing only in name and measure callback rates. The design is well established across many labour markets.
details.notes: The METHOD is well established; I have not verified an Iranian-specific study here. Layer-5 target: locate audit studies covering Iranian or Persian names specifically, rather than generalising from Arab/Muslim-name studies, which is a different population.

details.description: Many people adopt a shortened or Anglicised name on the CV. Where it works, it is evidence the discrimination was real; the cost is carried privately.
details.energy_note: Editing your own name to be employable.

details.description: An applicant delayed two years by security screening also carries an unexplained employment gap, which is independently penalised.

Omid's CV has a 26-month gap where a security screening ran. Every interviewer asks about it. 'I was waiting for a government decision' sounds, to a hiring manager who has never waited for one, like an evasion.
details.energy_note: Penalised twice: once for the delay, once for having to describe it.

details.description: Worldwide experimental data show minority-signalling candidates receive on average 29% fewer positive responses, with penalties as high as 41% for Arab applicants and as low as 8% for Hispanic applicants. Middle Easterners consistently rank among the most penalised groups.
details.energy_note: Not a feeling. A measured coefficient.
details.notes: ANSWERS EMP-003-001, partly. See the row below for the Iranian-specific gap.

details.aspect: NO study isolates Persian or Iranian names
details.description: Audit studies fold Iranians into a broad 'Middle Eastern' or 'Arab/Muslim' treatment. There is no dedicated experiment separating Persian names - a real limitation, given Iranians are not Arab.
details.energy_note: Measured as a category you are not a member of.
details.notes: ANSWERS EMP-003-001. This is also the empirical version of PSY-009: the conflation is not only cultural, it is baked into the research.

details.description: Candidates with Swedish names received 50% more callbacks than those with Middle Eastern names.

A large audit using Anglo-Saxon, Indigenous, Italian, Chinese and Middle Eastern names on otherwise identical entry-level CVs - all showing Australian schooling - found economically and statistically significant callback differences, with Italians facing less discrimination than Chinese and Middle Easterners.

Using a Bertrand-Mullainathan design, résumés with Arabic names received fewer callbacks than white-sounding names. Derous et al. (2009) found moderate discrimination against Arabic names in a résumé-sorting task.

Applicants are less likely to be called back when their names are difficult to pronounce - a finding that holds within immigrant groups, so it operates independently of ethnic animus. Persian names vary widely in distinctiveness and pronounceability, from Reza to Darius.
details.energy_note: Penalised for the number of syllables.
details.source_name: Hamilton College working paper on name pronunciation

details.aspect: Callback gaps understate the real gap
details.description: Quillian et al. (2020) document larger majority-minority differences at the job-offer stage than at callback - so audit studies, which measure only the first screen, are conservative estimates.

Darolia et al. (2016) found no callback discrimination across 9,000 résumés when pairing typically-white first names with typically-black last names - though critics argue the name signals may have been misread nearly 60% of the time. The debate about signal strength applies directly to Persian names.
details.notes: Included for balance. The effect is well established; the magnitude is genuinely contested.

issues.title: Blaine, January 2020 - detained for ancestry
issues.category_name: Borders, airports and secondary inspection
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Over a weekend in January 2020, US citizens and permanent residents of Iranian heritage were held for hours at the Peace Arch crossing and questioned about their politics and allegiance. Internal guidance later showed selection by nationality and birth year.

details.description: Over 4-5 January 2020, days after the killing of Qasem Soleimani, CBP held more than 60 American citizens and green card holders of Iranian heritage at Blaine, Washington, for up to 11-12 hours, questioning them about family, politics and allegiance to Iran.
details.time_note: Up to 12 hours in a single day.
details.energy_note: Questioned on loyalty as a citizen of the country doing the questioning.

details.description: A January 2020 Senate letter cited more than 60 held and up to 200 affected. A November 2021 congressional letter revised this to more than 80 held on 5 January 2020 with nearly 300 affected, some held over 10 hours and others turned away for lack of space.

Documents released under litigation - 237 pages ordered released by Chief Judge Ricardo Martinez - included a 7 January email stating the Seattle Field Office advised ports to refer all encounters with individuals 'from areas of national concern' to secondary. Proposed guidance required secondary inspection for individuals born after 1961 and before 2001 who met criteria including being 'Iranian and Lebanese nationals'.
details.energy_note: Nationality plus birth year, in writing.
details.notes: This and the NSIRA finding (SEC-001) are the two hardest documentary anchors in the dataset: both show selection by demographic category.

details.description: CBP stated it did not detain anyone because of country of origin, which first-hand accounts and the released records contradict. Lawmakers noted that traffic and staffing explanations did not account for why those affected were overwhelmingly of Iranian heritage or why pre-cleared travellers were delayed.
details.energy_note: Officially told the thing that happened to you did not happen.

details.description: Those held included NEXUS trusted-traveller holders, who had already passed background vetting, and were asked about political views, allegiances and ties to the Iranian military.
details.energy_note: Pre-clearance bought nothing.

details.description: The lasting cost is behavioural: people stop crossing, stop travelling, stop visiting relatives in Canada. A single weekend reshapes years of movement.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - turned away for lack of space
details.description: Some travellers were not merely delayed but turned away because the secondary inspection area had no room left.
details.energy_note: Refused entry to your own country because the queue was full.

details.description: An immigration attorney present reported a CBP officer describing it as 'extreme vetting', saying every Iranian was being sent to the port director for a final decision.
Those held included US citizens, permanent residents and people of all ages including the elderly and children.

issues.title: Routine secondary inspection and device searches
issues.category_name: Borders, airports and secondary inspection
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Outside headline incidents, Iranian travellers report disproportionate secondary inspection, questioning about family and politics, and searches of phones and laptops at the border, where normal warrant protections are weakest.

details.description: Device searches at the border operate under a reduced-protection doctrine in several countries, so a traveller can be required to unlock a phone with no suspicion standard that would be required inland.

details.aspect: What is on an Iranian's phone
details.description: Contacts in Iran, Persian-language messaging groups, VPN apps and family photos all read as flags to an officer working from a threat template.
details.energy_note: Ordinary life as suspicious material.

details.description: Hours in secondary routinely cost the onward flight.
details.money_note: Rebooking, hotel, lost accommodation.

details.aspect: Refusing is not an option in practice
details.description: Declining to unlock can mean device seizure for weeks, or denial of entry for a non-citizen. Consent is nominal.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the phone he had to unlock
details.description: Returning from Istanbul, Omid is sent to secondary. An officer asks him to unlock his phone. It contains a Telegram group of eighteen relatives, photographs of a protest he walked past in 2022, and a VPN app he uses to read the news. He unlocks it, because the alternative is a seized device and a missed connection.
details.money_note: Missed connection and one hotel night.
details.energy_note: Consent, offered at the only price available.

issues.title: Years of conditional status before anything is secure
issues.category_name: Status, residency and citizenship timelines
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by any immigrant regardless of origin
issues.summary: Between arrival and citizenship sit years of permits that must be renewed, each renewal a point at which the whole life can be refused.

details.description: Canada: 3 years of physical presence in 5 after PR. US: 5 years as LPR (3 if married to a citizen). UK: 5 years plus 12 months settled. Germany: reformed in 2024 to 5 years, or 3 with strong integration.
details.notes: Verify current rules; several changed between 2024 and 2026.

details.aspect: Processing sits on top of residence
details.description: The residence clock is the floor. Application processing adds months to years, and for Iranian applicants security screening adds more (see SEC-002).
Each permit renewal re-opens the file. Job loss, relationship breakdown or a policy change between renewals can end the whole project.
details.energy_note: Never being able to assume next year.

details.aspect: The cost of not being able to plan
details.description: Conditional status suppresses mortgage access, career risk-taking and family decisions. The measurable cost is small; the compounding life cost is not.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the renewal that catches the policy change
details.description: Permits are renewed against the rules in force on the renewal date, not the rules relied on when the life was built - so a policy change lands on whoever happens to be renewing that month.
details.energy_note: Rules changed under you, retrospectively in effect.

details.description: Lenders price or refuse on the remaining length of a residence permit, so a family pays rent for a decade while being creditworthy throughout.
details.money_note: Rent paid where a mortgage was affordable - illustrative.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the mortgage and the permit
details.description: Omid and Maryam have a 20% deposit and two salaries. The lender's policy requires at least twelve months remaining on the permit; theirs has nine. They renew, wait, reapply at eleven months remaining, and are told the policy changed in March to eighteen. They rent for three more years.
details.money_note: Rent paid over three years where a mortgage was affordable.

issues.title: Iran does not let citizenship go
issues.category_name: Status, residency and citizenship timelines
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Iran does not recognise renunciation in practice and treats dual nationals as Iranian only. Naturalising elsewhere does not end the Iranian obligations - including, for men, military service.

details.description: Renunciation requires government approval that is rarely granted, so Iranian nationality is effectively permanent.

details.aspect: Dual nationals treated as Iranian only
details.description: Inside Iran, the second passport confers nothing - no consular access, no protection. The foreign citizenship a person spent a decade earning stops at the border.
details.energy_note: Ten years of work, void on arrival.
details.notes: Standard travel-advisory language from multiple governments.

details.description: Several governments advise dual nationals against travel to Iran because of the risk of arbitrary detention.
details.notes: Layer-5 target: cite the specific FCDO / Global Affairs Canada / US State Department advisory text and date.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the citizenship that stops at the border
details.description: Nasrin becomes a Canadian citizen in 2025. Her Iranian nationality cannot be renounced in practice. If she enters Iran she enters as an Iranian, with no consular access. Her Canadian passport, which took nine years, is a document she cannot use in the one country she might need it.
details.energy_note: Nine years of work, void at one border.

details.description: Global Affairs Canada: avoid all travel; 'you should leave Iran now'. Canadians including dual Canadian-Iranian citizens are at high risk of arbitrary arrest and detention, and HOLDING A CANADIAN PASSPORT CAN BE REASON ENOUGH to detain you. Canada has no embassy or consulate in Iran.
details.energy_note: The passport you spent a decade earning is itself the risk factor.
details.source_name: Global Affairs Canada travel advice - Iran
details.notes: ANSWERS STA-002-003.

details.description: Level 4 - Do Not Travel. Iran does not recognise dual nationality and treats US-Iranian dual nationals solely as Iranian citizens, and DUAL NATIONALS MUST EXIT IRAN ON IRANIAN PASSPORTS. Some US nationals have been held for years on false charges, tortured, and sentenced to death. As of 15 October 2025 routine consular services are no longer available.
details.energy_note: You may only leave on the passport that requires military clearance.
details.notes: Connects MIL-004 to STA-002: exit requires an Iranian passport, and an Iranian passport requires the service card.

details.description: Smartraveller: do not travel. Foreigners including Australians and dual nationals are at high risk of arbitrary detention, have been detained without due process, consular access and legal representation cannot be guaranteed, and THE AUSTRALIAN GOVERNMENT MAY NOT BE NOTIFIED of a detention at all.
details.energy_note: Detained, and nobody who could help is told.

details.description: Canada's advisory states plainly that Iranian authorities arrest and detain individuals 'including foreign and dual nationals, to exert political or diplomatic influence on their governments' - naming the practice as leverage rather than law enforcement.
details.energy_note: A person used as a message between states.

issues.title: Parents cannot visit
issues.category_name: Family, reunification and visitors
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Visitor visas for Iranian parents are refused at high rates on 'ties' and 'intent' grounds. The practical effect is that grandparents never meet grandchildren and nobody attends anybody's funeral.

details.description: Elderly applicants with adult children abroad are assessed as likely to overstay. The very fact that establishes the reason to visit is the reason for refusal.
details.energy_note: Family ties recast as immigration risk.

details.description: Each refusal costs the fee and must be declared on the next application, so persistence makes success less likely.
details.money_note: Fees plus travel to a third country to apply.

details.description: Under the 2026 US full suspension, an Iranian parent cannot attend a child's graduation, wedding or funeral. The loss is not recoverable later.
details.energy_note: The one cost nobody can be compensated for.

details.description: A couple marrying abroad, where neither set of parents can obtain a visitor visa, either marries without family or does not marry.
details.energy_note: Your parents watch on a phone screen.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the grandparent who never meets the child
details.description: Under the January 2026 US suspension there is no visitor route at all, so a grandchild born in 2026 may not meet a grandparent before that grandparent dies.
details.energy_note: A person who will die before meeting their grandchild.

details.description: Omid and Maryam marry in Toronto in 2026. Both sets of parents apply for visitor visas. All four are refused: insufficient ties, and an adult child resident in Canada. The ceremony has eleven guests, nine of whom the couple met after arriving.
details.energy_note: Married in a room with no one who watched you grow up.

issues.title: Locked out of the tools of the trade
issues.category_name: Technology, platforms and digital exclusion
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: US platforms blocked Iranian users on sanctions grounds - including users who had left Iran years earlier - cutting off source control, cloud, payments and app distribution.

details.description: GitHub restricted users in Iran, Syria and Crimea, suspending private repositories and paid services. Restrictions were applied by IP address and payment history, with warnings against using VPNs to disguise location.
details.energy_note: Your own code, behind a wall.

details.description: Iranians reported receiving emails that their AWS accounts had been disabled for sanctions compliance. Developers lost academic work and running applications stopped.

details.aspect: Slack, December 2018 - people who had already left
details.description: Slack deactivated accounts of Iranians even where they had left Iran, and apologised after international coverage for deactivating accounts it should not have.
details.energy_note: Punished for where you were born, years after leaving.

details.aspect: The appeal is a selfie and a passport
details.description: Users wrongly suspended could appeal by supplying government photo ID and a selfie to prove residency - proving a negative about where you are not.
details.energy_note: Identity documents demanded by a private company.

details.description: Stripe, PayPal and the major US processors are unavailable, so Iranian freelancers and open-source contributors have no legitimate route to receive international payment. Apple and Google developer accounts are also restricted.
details.money_note: Income foregone; unquantified.

details.description: The Internet Society notes the technical ramifications extend far beyond the intended scope. GitHub rolled back some restrictions after criticism - which confirms they were broader than required.

The alternatives are Iranian infrastructure, which is censored and surveilled, or diaspora family accounts and VPNs, which breach the platforms' terms and risk permanent ban. There is no compliant option.
details.energy_note: Every available choice is against some rule.

details.description: GitHub's restrictions keyed off IP address AND PAYMENT HISTORY - so a card once used from Iran could mark an account years later and anywhere.
details.energy_note: A five-year-old transaction as evidence of residence.

details.description: Users who had merely VISITED Iran reported being caught in the dragnet and having to appeal with documents proving they were not based there.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the account he built for six years
details.description: Reza's GitHub holds six years of commits, two libraries with real users, and the portfolio that gets him interviews. In 2019 his private repositories are restricted; the appeal form asks for a government photo ID and a selfie. He has lived in Berlin for four months. He sends both to a company he has never spoken to.
details.energy_note: Handing your passport to a website to get your own work back.

issues.title: Everyday nationality friction
issues.category_name: Discrimination and daily life
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Car hire, insurance, tenancy screening, payment processors and background-check vendors all run sanctions screens. Each one occasionally returns a false positive on an Iranian name or birthplace, and each must be argued individually.

details.description: Sanctions screening is embedded in ordinary commercial onboarding, not just banking.
Common Persian names collide with sanctions-list entries, producing repeated manual review the customer must resolve by proving who they are not.
Refusals cite internal policy. Without a stated reason there is nothing to appeal and no evidence of a pattern.
details.energy_note: Unfalsifiable, therefore unchallengeable.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the name that trips the screen
