details.description: Common Persian names collide with sanctions-list entries, so an ordinary purchase, tenancy check or payroll onboarding drops into manual review and the customer must prove they are not a listed person.
details.energy_note: Proving a negative about a stranger with your name.

details.description: Rental and insurance underwriting runs sanctions and residency screens; a licence issued in Iran or a birthplace field reading Tehran can produce a refusal with no stated reason and no appeal.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the car hire in Munich
details.description: Reza books a car for a client visit. At the desk his Iranian-issued licence and birthplace trigger a review. The agent is apologetic and says the system will not let her proceed. He takes three trains, arrives ninety minutes late, and explains the delay as traffic.
details.energy_note: Lying about small humiliations to stay professional.

issues.title: The cost of indefinite uncertainty
issues.category_name: Health, mental load and the cost of uncertainty
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by any immigrant regardless of origin
issues.summary: Years of pending status with no decision date is a documented stressor distinct from a bad outcome. Waiting without a deadline is the specific harm.

details.description: The distinguishing feature of immigration limbo is the absence of a date. Plans cannot be made and grief cannot be finished.
Children, property, career moves and elderly-parent care are all postponed pending a decision that does not come.
Counselling is often outside basic coverage for temporary residents.
details.money_note: Out-of-pocket where not covered.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - lives held open for a decade
details.description: Students in the Vice report described putting personal and professional lives on hold for up to ten years - missing job opportunities, conferences and family weddings, not because of a refusal but because no answer ever came.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the decisions he stopped making
details.description: By month 20 Omid has stopped buying furniture, stopped going to the dentist and stopped replying to a woman he liked, because he cannot answer the question 'where will you be next year'. He is not depressed and he is not fine. There is no word for it and no box for it on any form.
details.energy_note: A life on hold is not a life, and does not count as a harm.

details.description: The bandwidth research is the measured version of what HLT-001 describes qualitatively: uncertainty is not merely unpleasant, it consumes the cognitive capacity that planning and problem-solving run on, by about a standard deviation.

issues.title: Legal help is expensive and mostly unavailable
issues.category_name: Asylum, legal process and representation
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by any immigrant regardless of origin
issues.summary: Immigration law is complex, consequential and largely outside legal aid. Most people navigate it alone or pay heavily.

details.description: Skilled-migration application assistance commonly runs USD 1,500-6,000; litigation such as mandamus USD 3,000-12,000; complex or appeal work more.
Diaspora communities are heavily targeted by unlicensed agents. Money is lost and, worse, a badly prepared application creates a refusal that follows the applicant permanently.
details.energy_note: Defrauded while trying to comply.

details.description: Applicants prefer Persian-speaking advisers, which shrinks the market and raises the chance of ending up with whoever is available rather than whoever is good.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the consultant who was not licensed
details.description: Diaspora communities are heavily targeted by unlicensed agents. The damage is rarely just the fee: a badly prepared or dishonest application produces a refusal, and misrepresentation findings carry multi-year bans that follow the applicant everywhere.
details.energy_note: Defrauded, then punished for the fraud.

issues.title: The one-way door
issues.category_name: Return, exit and the one-way-door problem
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Iranian nationality and being male
issues.summary: For many Iranian men the decision to leave is effectively irreversible: conscription liability, political exposure or asylum claim all make return unsafe or impossible. Every other hurdle is faced with no fallback.

details.description: Claiming protection from a state is incompatible with returning to it. Re-availment can void the status granted.
details.energy_note: Safety purchased with permanent exile.

details.aspect: Conscription liability does the same without a claim
details.description: A man who never served faces detention or forced service on return, so the door closes even for someone with no political profile.
Most migrants can go home if it does not work. Removing that option changes every calculation: a bad job, a bad marriage, a bad city must be endured.
details.energy_note: No exit from the exit.

details.description: The concrete form this takes is a parent dying while the son cannot attend. It recurs in Iranian diaspora accounts more than any other single loss.
details.notes: For narrative use: this is the emotional centre of the whole dataset.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the estate you cannot settle
details.description: A DOHA applicant refused to surrender his Iranian passport because he needed it to settle his father's estate in Iran, and lost his clearance for it. Returning for a death in the family and keeping a career were incompatible.

Nasrin calls at four in the morning. Their father has had a stroke and is in Sina Hospital. Omid has not served. If he goes he may not come back; if he does not go he may not see his father again. He is on the phone to an immigration lawyer by six and at his desk by nine, because there is nothing to decide.
details.energy_note: The decision that is not a decision, because one option does not exist.

issues.title: Selectee screening at US airports
issues.category_name: Borders, airports and secondary inspection
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Beyond land borders, Iranian travellers report being marked SSSS on boarding passes far more often than chance would suggest. The mechanism is documented; the selection rates are secret.

details.description: Secure Flight marks selected passengers with SSSS (or S) on the boarding pass, triggering enhanced screening - intensive search, enhanced pat-down, sometimes powering on every device. It can happen at the checkpoint, a separate area, or at the gate, and applies to flights to, from, within and overflying the US.
details.source_name: TSA Secure Flight / Secondary Security Screening Selection

details.description: There is no public statistic on SSSS designation rates for Iranian travellers. The documented profiling evidence is land-border, not airport.
details.energy_note: A pattern everyone experiences and nobody can measure.
details.notes: HONEST LIMIT: the disproportion is widely reported and NOT statistically established. ACLU/CAIR/NIAC FOIA records are the place to dig - layer-5 target.

details.description: In January 2020, lawmakers asked CBP whether officers had questioned US travellers at airports, and requested any directives on 'the screening of individuals of Iranian heritage' after Soleimani's killing - indicating the concern was not confined to Blaine.
Arrive hours early every flight, keep every device charged, expect to miss tight connections. For frequent flyers the cumulative cost is days per year.
details.money_note: Missed connections, rebooking, extra nights.
details.time_note: Per flight; compounding across a year.
details.source_name: The Points Guy - the dreaded SSSS

details.description: DHS TRIP exists for redress, but a selectee is never told why they were selected, so there is nothing specific to rebut.
details.energy_note: Appeal against an unstated reason.

details.description: Senators recorded that people subjected to prolonged inspection - including US citizens and permanent residents - were asked about political views, allegiances, social media profiles, family relationships and military service.
details.energy_note: Your own citizenship does not end the interrogation.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - eleven SSSS in fourteen flights
details.description: Omid keeps a note in his phone. Across fourteen flights in two years his boarding pass was stamped SSSS eleven times. He now books the earliest flight of the day and arrives three and a half hours early, every time, and has stopped booking connections under two hours.
details.time_note: About 45 hours a year in extra airport time.
details.energy_note: A private statistic nobody will accept as evidence.

issues.title: The air route itself keeps disappearing
issues.category_name: Visas, permits and the right to arrive
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Direct flights between Iran and Europe have repeatedly been suspended - by sanctions, by safety, by war and by single incidents. Each suspension strands people mid-journey and forces longer, costlier routings.

details.aspect: October 2022 - Lufthansa and Austrian suspend Iran flights
details.description: A body was found in the undercarriage of an Airbus A340 at Frankfurt after it arrived from Tehran as flight LH 601 and had been moved to a hangar. Lufthansa suspended Tehran flights pending clarification and cancelled the next day's service; Austrian Airlines also cancelled Iran flights.
details.money_note: Rebooking and accommodation.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - held, marched and put on a replacement aircraft
details.description: In 2022 Lufthansa held back an aircraft on the Iran route. Passengers, including elderly travellers, were made to walk a long distance to a poor-quality holding facility, waited there, and were eventually flown out on an unscheduled replacement aircraft.
details.energy_note: The indignity is the point - it is not what happens on other routes.
details.notes: Account as related; no press report located. The adjacent documented event is the October 2022 suspension in the row above.

details.aspect: Sanctions ground the domestic fleet too
details.description: Iranian carriers cannot buy aircraft or certified spare parts, so the domestic and regional fleet is old and unreliable, and foreign carriers are the only dependable option - until they leave.

details.aspect: Longer routings cost money and visas
details.description: Without direct flights, routings go via Istanbul, Doha or Dubai - which means transit rules, sometimes transit visas, and for the UAE a visa an Iranian may not get.
Regional conflict has repeatedly closed Iranian airspace at short notice, stranding travellers mid-route with no rebooking path home.
details.notes: Airspace closures during the June 2025 hostilities are widely reported; specific dates and passenger impact need verification.

details.description: A Lufthansa 747 diverted to Istanbul and sat for 34 hours. Long diversions on this corridor are common enough to have their own genre of account.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - trapped on the aircraft overnight
details.description: In a separate Lufthansa case, passengers were kept aboard all night after a cancellation because the airport had closed around them.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - 45 hours, seniors and infants, no assistance
details.description: Lufthansa LH754 Frankfurt-Bengaluru diverted to Istanbul and arrived over 45 hours late. Passengers including senior citizens and infants were stranded at Istanbul reportedly without airline assistance, kept on the plane four hours, then left without proper updates. Lufthansa said oxygen cylinders used in a medical emergency had to be replaced and it took longer than expected.
details.notes: Not an Iran route, but the closest documented match for the pattern of elderly passengers stranded through a Lufthansa diversion.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the rebooking that cost more than the ticket
details.description: Hassan is booked Tehran-Frankfurt-Toronto to meet his grandson. Lufthansa suspends the Tehran route with nine days' notice. The only rerouting is via Istanbul and Doha, 31 hours, and the fare difference is USD 1,150. He is 58 and has never flown more than five hours.

issues.title: The English test itself became unavailable
issues.category_name: Education, credentials and academic recognition
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: In 2026 the standard English proficiency tests stopped being offered inside Iran - IELTS in January, then TOEFL, GRE and Duolingo after OFAC suspended the licence that permitted educational services to Iranians.

details.description: OFAC indefinitely suspended General License G on 24 August 2026. Since 2014 that licence had been the legal basis for US universities and testing companies to provide educational services to Iranians. Wind-down transactions were allowed until 8 September 2026.
details.energy_note: The ladder out of the country withdrawn in a single administrative act.

details.description: ETS told Radio Farda it had 'paused administration of the TOEFL and GRE tests in Iran effective immediately'. Appointment calendars bookable as far out as January shrank within a day to two centres near Tehran, then vanished.

IELTS testing inside Iran ended on 31 January 2026 after IDP cited financial and regulatory factors outside its control. IELTS is British/Australian, not American, so the OFAC suspension does not explain it - the withdrawal was independent.
details.notes: Two separate mechanisms arriving at the same result within seven months.

details.aspect: Duolingo cut off by identity document
details.description: The Duolingo English Test announced it would cease serving individuals residing in Iran OR HOLDING IRANIAN IDENTIFICATION DOCUMENTS from 1 September 2026 - so the restriction follows the passport, not the address.
details.energy_note: Excluded by nationality even if you left years ago.

details.description: ETS says Iranians may travel abroad to sit the exams. That means flights and at least one night's accommodation in Turkey or Armenia on top of the fee - for a test that is itself a precondition of a scholarship application.
details.money_note: Travel, accommodation, fee, exchange loss.

details.description: The United States fully suspended visa issuance to Iranian nationals across nearly all categories from 1 January 2026. Students are therefore paying to travel abroad to sit a test for a country that will not issue them a visa.
details.energy_note: Effort with no possible destination.

details.description: Iranian TOEFL and GRE candidates launched an online petition urging ETS to restore access, saying thousands were losing access to tests required for admissions and scholarships.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the test that moved to another country
details.description: Maryam needs IELTS 7.0 for her licensing pathway. Testing in Iran ended in January. The nearest centre is Yerevan: flight USD 280, two nights USD 90, test fee USD 250, and a day either side. She needs 7.0 in writing and gets 6.5. She books again.
details.money_note: Two attempts, travel included.

issues.title: ATAS: refused with no reason given
issues.category_name: Education, credentials and academic recognition
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Iranian postgraduates in UK STEM subjects must obtain ATAS clearance. Iran is not on the exemption list, refusals are not explained, and a refusal blocks the visa entirely.

details.description: ATAS checks international postgraduates in science and technology subjects. Nationals of certain exempt countries are excused; Iran is not among them, so Iranian STEM postgraduates are routinely required to clear it.
For national security reasons the ATAS team will not explain to the applicant or the university why clearance was refused, so institutions cannot advise on or address the concern.
details.energy_note: Refused, with nothing to fix.

details.description: If a course requires ATAS and it is refused, the student visa will not be granted and the applicant cannot enrol.
After refusal the applicant must wait 90 days before reapplying for the same course or research area at the same institution under the same CAH3 code - which usually means missing the academic year.

A UK academic posted publicly about an Iranian applicant refused ATAS for the third time after more than four months of waiting, describing the security-focused system as disproportionately rejecting Iranian applicants.
details.source_name: Public LinkedIn post by a UK academic
details.notes: Advocacy commentary from a named academic, not data. Treat as testimony.

details.description: Universities say refusals are 'rare' but publish nothing by nationality. Figures would have to come from an FCDO Freedom of Information response or a parliamentary written answer.
details.energy_note: The disproportion cannot be proven from public data.
details.notes: LAYER-5 TARGET: FOI request to FCDO for ATAS refusals by nationality.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - refused, reapply in 90 days, miss the year
details.description: Omid holds an offer for a materials PhD at Manchester starting September. ATAS is refused in June with no reason. He must wait 90 days to reapply for the same research area. The 90 days end in September. The studentship is annual.
details.energy_note: A wait engineered to be exactly longer than the thing you are waiting for.

details.aspect: Why the statistics do not exist
details.description: The FCDO will not disclose ATAS refusal reasons to applicant or university, citing the sensitivity of the clearance. Nationality-level breakdowns have historically been resisted under FOI section 24 (national security) and section 27 (international relations).
details.energy_note: The disproportion cannot be measured, by design.
details.notes: PARTLY ANSWERS EDU-005-006: the answer is that the data is withheld, not that it does not exist. Direct routes remain WhatDoTheyKnow, the FCDO disclosure log, and parliamentary written questions.

details.aspect: Two refusals can end the offer
details.description: Reapplying after a refusal is usually unsuccessful, and two refusals can lead to withdrawal of the study offer altogether - so the 90-day bar is not the worst of it.
details.energy_note: Two unexplained noes and the place is gone.

details.description: Iranian applicants on UK student forums circulate the claim that ATAS is rejecting Iranian applications because of US sanctions. No official source confirms it. The belief itself shapes where people apply.
details.energy_note: In the absence of reasons, people build their own.

issues.title: Sanctioned universities: the degree carries the designation
issues.category_name: Education, credentials and academic recognition
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Sharif University of Technology - Iran's leading engineering school - has been sanctioned by the EU, UK and Japan. Its graduates carry the association through every subsequent visa, job and clearance check.

details.description: The EU listed Sharif on 22 December 2012 as linked to proliferation-sensitive nuclear activity or nuclear weapon delivery systems. The General Court annulled the listing on 3 July 2014. It was relisted on 7 November 2014.
details.energy_note: Even a court annulment did not end it - relisted four months later.
details.source_name: Iran Watch - Sharif University of Technology

details.description: The UK sanctioned the university on 31 December 2020, freezing assets and restricting transactions. It had previously been listed in 2015 as an entity of potential WMD-procurement concern and removed in 2017 when the UK withdrew its Iran list. Japan listed it in 2022.

Designations rest on cooperation agreements with UN/EU-designated Iranian organisations in military fields, including the Ministry of Defence, the IRGC and the IRGC Air Force, and the Aerospace Industries Organization.

details.aspect: Institutional designation is NOT a rule about students
details.description: Entity and asset-freeze designations apply to the institution as a transacting party - export licensing and financial transactions. They are legally distinct from visa policy affecting individual students or alumni, which runs through separate consular authorities.
details.energy_note: Important: the law does not say what employers think it says.
details.notes: Worth knowing in an argument. The conflation is common and wrong.

details.aspect: But the association follows the CV anyway
details.description: A Sharif degree names a sanctioned entity on every application form. Whether or not any rule requires it, screeners react to the name.
details.energy_note: A permanent mark acquired at eighteen by being admitted to the best engineering school in the country.

details.description: Sharif had roughly 10,800 students as of autumn 2022 across 13 science and engineering departments - so each cohort adds thousands of people carrying the designation.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the alma mater on every form
details.description: Reza graduated from Sharif in 2013 in computer engineering. He has never been in a laboratory. Every visa form, every background check and every bank onboarding asks where he studied, and the answer is an entity on three sanctions lists. He has started writing 'Tehran' and the year, and waiting to be asked.
details.energy_note: A truthful answer that costs you something every time.

issues.title: IRGC conscription and Canadian inadmissibility
issues.category_name: Military service and the male exit problem
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Iranian nationality and being male
issues.summary: Canada listed the IRGC as a terrorist entity in June 2024. Men who were conscripted into IRGC-affiliated units - an assignment they did not choose - now face inadmissibility for 'membership' in a listed entity.

details.description: On 19 June 2024 Public Safety Minister Dominic LeBlanc announced the IRGC was listed as a terrorist entity under the Criminal Code, effective that day.

IRPA s.34(1)(f) makes a person inadmissible on security grounds for being a member of an organisation there are reasonable grounds to believe engages in terrorism. A finding can rest on an admission, documents or service records.
details.energy_note: Your own honest answer on a form becomes the evidence.

details.description: In Vadiati the Court held conscript service could establish membership for s.34(1)(f), following the established approach that membership does not require ideological commitment or involvement in any specific act.
details.energy_note: Conscription and enlistment treated alike.
details.notes: Verify Vadiati directly (Federal Court) before citing - this is a practitioner summary.

details.description: In July 2024 the Minister amended the start date of the Iranian regime designation to 23 June 2003, so senior officials who served at any time since then may be barred, and those already in Canada investigated and removed.
details.energy_note: A rule written in 2024 reaching back twenty-one years.

details.description: Men who did compulsory service and were assigned to the Sepah may receive a Procedural Fairness Letter questioning admissibility - the first many hear of it, often years into an application.
details.money_note: Legal representation to answer the PFL.

details.aspect: The government says it is individual; an MP says otherwise
details.description: IRCC states that 'membership in the IRGC and service in the IRGC are distinct considerations' and that applications are assessed individually. In November Canada said it does not automatically reject PR applications solely for compulsory service - after a conscript said he had been ruled inadmissible for involuntary service.
details.energy_note: Reassurance issued only after the thing it denies had happened.

details.description: MP Garnett Genuis said the government failed to protect those forced into conscription - 'We shouldn't be punishing victims of forced conscription' - and proposed targeting instead those who volunteered, stayed on, or committed atrocities, suggesting a legislative exemption as the fastest fix.

details.aspect: The defence got weaker, not stronger
details.description: A practitioner guide notes 'the honest picture changed in 2025', with older defensive arguments having weakened - so a man whose case was arguable in 2024 may not be arguable now.
details.energy_note: The ground moving under a case already filed.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the two years he cannot explain away
details.description: Omid served 2019-21. His unit was a Basij-affiliated logistics depot outside Karaj; he drove a truck and did inventory. In 2025 IRCC sends a procedural fairness letter asking him to address possible inadmissibility under s.34(1)(f). He is asked to prove a negative about an assignment he was given at nineteen by a lottery.
details.energy_note: Asked to disprove a posting you never chose.

issues.title: German asylum decisions on Iran got harsher as Iran got worse
issues.category_name: Asylum, legal process and representation
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Germany's protection rate for substantively examined Iranian claims fell from 45% to 27% between 2023 and 2025, while repression inside Iran intensified. Men fare worse than women.

details.description: PRO ASYL documents the adjusted protection rate (bereinigte Schutzquote) for Iran falling from 45% in 2023 to 37% in 2024 to 27% in 2025. Three-quarters of substantively examined Iranian claims were rejected in 2025.
details.source_name: PRO ASYL policy paper on Iran decisions

details.description: Positive decisions ran at 30% for women and 25% for men - a five-point gap, with both far below the rate of a few years earlier.
details.energy_note: A measurable male penalty, in a published figure.
details.notes: One of the very few places a male-specific disadvantage is actually quantified in official-derived data. High value.

details.description: PRO ASYL identifies: questionable distinctions between protest organisers and participants; unclear reasoning about what exit from Iran was possible; and dismissal of sexualised violence as 'alleged isolated incidents'.
German courts corrected BAMF decisions thousands of times in 2025, granting protection contrary to the original rejection. For Iranian applicants the overturn rate was around 54% in 2023.
details.time_note: An appeal adds years on top of the original wait.
details.energy_note: Right eventually, after years - if you can fund the appeal.

details.description: The organisation describes a stark contradiction - 'mass arrests, torture, sexualized violence, and increasing executions' intensifying in 2025-2026 while approval rates fell - and suggests quotas may be 'deliberately kept low for domestic political reasons'.
details.notes: This is an advocacy organisation's interpretation, clearly labelled as such. The underlying rates are BAMF data.

details.description: Germany's overall protection rate fell from 51.7% (2023) to 44.4% (2024) to 28.1% (2025). Iran fell faster than the average.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - rejected, then granted on appeal, three years later
details.description: Reza's asylum claim is rejected by BAMF in 2024: the reasoning distinguishes protest organisers from participants and places him in the second group. He appeals. In 2027 the administrative court grants protection. He has spent three years unable to work at his profession, and has been right the whole time.
details.energy_note: Vindicated, three years after it would have helped.

issues.title: Getting money out legally, if you are a US person
issues.category_name: Banking, money movement and sanctions spillover
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: OFAC permits sale and transfer of inherited property or property owned before becoming a US person. Everything else needs a specific licence, and the routing runs through third countries.

details.description: Under OFAC 31 CFR 560.543, only property owned before becoming a US person, or property inherited, may be sold and proceeds transferred without special permission. All other cases require a specific OFAC licence.
US banks cannot process payments directly involving Iranian banks, so transfers route through non-SDN intermediaries in the UAE, Turkey, Oman or Qatar, with funds converted to euros or dirhams first.
details.money_note: Intermediary fees and FX spread.

details.description: Bypassing banking restrictions via crypto, hawala or unlicensed money transmitters has led to enforcement actions with asset freezes, large fines and imprisonment.
details.energy_note: The workaround everyone uses is also a felony.

details.description: Sale proceeds are deposited into a rial account that must then be converted to hard currency, and moving large foreign exchange out needs Central Bank approval. A property transfer tax of about 5% applies.
details.money_note: 5% transfer tax on sale price.

details.aspect: Inherited property cannot always be kept
details.description: A foreign national inheriting Iranian property gets valid ownership, but Iranian law does not permit indefinite foreign ownership - the heir is typically required to transfer it to a qualified person.
details.energy_note: Forced sale of the family home, on someone else's timetable.

details.aspect: And then the IRS wants to know
details.description: Cash inheritance over USD 100,000 from a foreign estate, or non-cash over that value, must be reported to the IRS. Gains on sales of non-commercial Iranian real estate are reportable in the year of sale.

issues.title: Iran charges you to leave, and limits what you take
issues.category_name: Banking, money movement and sanctions spillover
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Iranian nationality and being male
issues.summary: A tiered departure tax rises with each trip in a solar year, and hard limits cap the currency, gold and goods that may leave with you.

details.description: Iranian nationals must pay a departure tax before passport control, rising by trip number within the solar year: 1st ﷼9,000,000, 2nd ﷼15,000,000, 3rd ﷼22,000,000. Payable online in advance or at Bank Melli branches, with the slip shown to the passport police. Religious travel is taxed far less on second and subsequent departures.
details.energy_note: Leaving repeatedly is priced as suspicious behaviour.
details.notes: Rial figures move with budget cycles - verify before quoting.

details.description: A further levy added in 2024 applies to all passengers over two years old, is calculated at a government-controlled exchange rate, and exempts pilgrims to Iraq, Saudi Arabia and Syria. It sits on top of the ordinary duty - about 520,000 rials (roughly USD 8.80) for the year to March 2025.

Up to EUR 5,000 equivalent in cash or bank documents; above that needs Central Bank approval. Up to 150g of gold, silver or platinum jewellery and 3kg of non-antique silver. Iranian gold coins are prohibited from export under any circumstances. Up to 24 square metres of hand-woven carpet, 125g caviar, 150g saffron.
details.energy_note: A life's savings capped at what fits in a pocket.

details.description: Gold coins are the standard Iranian household savings instrument precisely because the currency is unstable - and they are the one thing absolutely barred from leaving.
details.energy_note: The savings vehicle that cannot emigrate with you.

details.aspect: Tax clearance as an exit condition
details.description: For foreigners, an exit visa typically requires a tax clearance certificate; failure to obtain one can result in travel restrictions and penalties. Tax residency arises after 183 days.

Hassan's savings are 40 Bahar Azadi gold coins, held since 2014 because the rial is not a savings vehicle. Coins may not be exported under any circumstances. He can take 150g of jewellery. He sells the coins at a bad rate to a dealer who knows he is leaving, and carries the loss out as a rounding error.
details.money_note: Distress-sale discount on the family savings.
details.energy_note: A lifetime of saving, discounted for being in a hurry.

issues.title: Housing, licences and the ordinary machinery of settling
issues.category_name: Discrimination and daily life
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by any immigrant regardless of origin
issues.summary: The unglamorous layer: finding a flat with no local credit history, exchanging a driving licence, enrolling children, and re-establishing every routine relationship that a settled person already has.

details.description: Landlords screen on credit file and local references. A new arrival has neither, so the options are a large deposit, a guarantor, or the informal market.
details.money_note: Additional deposit, agency fees, guarantor services.

details.description: Iran has reciprocal exchange arrangements with few destination countries, so most Iranians must re-sit theory and practical tests, often with a waiting list, and pay higher insurance as a 'new' driver despite decades of experience.
details.notes: Reciprocity lists are published per jurisdiction - verify per country. Layer-5 target.

details.aspect: Insurance priced on a blank history
details.description: No local claims history means the highest premium band for several years, regardless of actual record.
details.money_note: Excess premium over several years.

details.aspect: Children re-placed by language, not ability
details.description: Children are commonly placed by language proficiency rather than academic level, losing a year or more and the peer group with it.
details.energy_note: A child demoted for an accent.

details.description: Iranian social insurance contributions are not portable to any major destination, so working years already paid for are simply lost.
details.money_note: Foregone entitlement - illustrative, not measured.
details.notes: No totalisation agreement located between Iran and major destinations. Layer-5 target: confirm per country.

issues.title: Nationality passes down, and so does the obligation
issues.category_name: Family, reunification and visitors
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Iranian nationality and being male
issues.summary: Iranian nationality descends from the father. A man who emigrates and has sons abroad passes them Iranian nationality - and with it, in principle, the conscription liability he left to escape.

details.description: Iranian nationality law is principally patrilineal: a child of an Iranian father is Iranian regardless of birthplace.
details.notes: Well established in outline; cite the Civil Code article directly before relying on it.

details.description: A son born abroad to an Iranian father is, in Iranian law, an Iranian male - and therefore in principle liable for military service if he ever enters Iran on an Iranian passport.
details.energy_note: Passing on a liability you fled, to a child who has never been there.
details.notes: Enforcement against the never-resident is unclear and varies. Layer-5 target: consular practice for foreign-born sons.

details.aspect: The asymmetry runs the other way for mothers
details.description: Until a 2019 reform, Iranian women could not pass nationality to children of foreign fathers. Recording this because the dataset should be accurate about gender rather than one-directional: some Iranian gender burdens fall on women, and this one did.
details.notes: Included deliberately for balance and credibility.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the son born in Toronto
details.description: Omid's son is born in Toronto in 2028. Under Iranian law he is an Iranian male through his father. If he ever enters Iran on an Iranian passport he is, in principle, a conscript. Omid registers the birth at the consulate anyway, because not doing so means the boy could never inherit the Tehran apartment.
details.energy_note: Passing on the trap, because refusing to costs him something else.

issues.title: Deported on arrival, holding a valid visa
issues.category_name: Borders, airports and secondary inspection
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Between 2019 and 2021 Iranian students who had passed a year of vetting, been granted visas and flown to the United States were detained at the airport, had their visas revoked on the spot, and were put on a plane home.

details.description: From August 2019 to January 2020 at least 16 Iranian students were detained and deported after arriving at US airports despite holding valid student visas. Boston Logan was the focal point - at least 10 sent back from August 2019, more than seven through Logan.
details.energy_note: Vetted, approved, flown, refused.
details.source_name: Deportation of Iranian students at US airports

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - Shahab Dehghani, deported against a court order
details.description: Dehghani arrived at Logan on 19 January 2020 to study at Northeastern. CBP detained and questioned him for hours then revoked the student visa the State Department had granted after a year of intense vetting. A federal judge issued an emergency stay delaying removal for two days. CBP put him on a flight to Iran anyway. His attorney said he was removed without access to his lawyer and without being told the basis.
details.money_note: Flights, tuition deposit, legal fees, lost year.
details.energy_note: A federal court order ignored in real time.

details.description: A DHS official later told WBUR that CBP denied Dehghani entry because they believed his immediate family had ties to the IRGC, and claimed family ties to a transport company sanctioned in 2010. His attorney denied any grounds of inadmissibility existed.
details.energy_note: Excluded for his relatives, told only via the press.

details.description: Crowds gathered at Boston Logan in protest while he was held, which did not stop the removal.

Attorney Susan Church also represented an Iranian student hoping to attend Harvard Divinity School who was denied entry at Logan in 2019. A 35-year-old traveller denied entry in September 2019 had her visa revoked and was placed on a removal flight.
Iranians turned away at the US border rose more than 150% from 2015 to 2019 - 736 to 1,895 - even as Iranian student and exchange visitors fell 43%. More refusals from a smaller pool.
A CBP spokesman said less than one percent of Iranian passengers arriving at Boston were deported in 2019 - a denominator chosen to make the number small.
details.energy_note: True, and beside the point.

details.aspect: It kept going under a new administration
details.description: A January 2021 Boston Globe investigation found the practice continuing via expedited removal, with Logan a hotbed of litigation over these cases.

details.aspect: The lawyers think the count is higher
details.description: The AILA New England chair suggested the real number could be as high as two dozen, because deportations are not always public.

details.aspect: Expedited removal carries a five-year bar
details.description: Removal at the border is not simply being sent home - expedited removal normally triggers a multi-year bar on return, so a single airport decision closes the country for years.
details.energy_note: One officer, one shift, five years.

issues.title: Refused service by private businesses
issues.category_name: Discrimination and daily life
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Shop staff, banks and platforms enforce sanctions themselves, at the counter, against customers who are lawfully present and often citizens. Speaking Persian in the wrong shop has been enough.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the Apple Store, Georgia, June 2012
details.description: Sahar Sabet, 19 and a US citizen, was refused an iPad at an Apple store in Georgia after an employee overheard her speaking Farsi with her uncle. She was told: 'I just can't sell this to you. Our countries have such bad relations.' She already owned an iPhone and a MacBook. She called it 'very hurtful, very embarrassing' and walked out in tears.
details.energy_note: Refused for the language you were speaking to your uncle.

details.description: When Sabet returned with a WSB-TV crew the same employee refused again, and the manager produced the sales policy stating Apple products must not be sold for export to Iran, North Korea or other embargoed countries.
details.energy_note: Policy read aloud to justify it.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - a second customer, a second store
details.description: Zack Jafarzadeh had the same experience at a different Apple store.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the employee was Iranian himself
details.description: The staff member recognised Farsi because he was from Iran. The enforcement ran through someone from the same community.
details.energy_note: Policed by your own.

details.aspect: There was no law requiring it
details.description: A State Department representative clarified there was no policy or law prohibiting Apple from selling in the US to anyone intending to use the goods in the US, including customers of Iranian descent or citizenship. A licence is needed only to take high-technology goods TO Iran.
details.energy_note: The refusal was not required by anything.

details.description: OFAC rules make a person liable for exporting goods they know or have reason to know are intended for Iran - which pushes the judgement down to the sales associate, who has civil and criminal exposure and no training. Overcaution is the rational individual response.
details.energy_note: The system delegates the discrimination to a 22-year-old on a till.

details.description: Sabet later received an apology from Apple customer relations and was told she could buy the iPad online. CAIR called on Apple to change the policy; NIAC's Jamal Abdi attacked the practice in a New York Times op-ed.
details.energy_note: Resolved privately, policy unchanged.

details.description: Omid goes to buy a laptop. The assistant asks where he is from, then asks a manager, then comes back and says the system needs an address verification they cannot complete today. He buys the same laptop online that evening, delivered to the same address.
details.energy_note: Refused in person, sold to online, by the same company.

issues.title: The appointment does not exist, and then it costs EUR 1,000
issues.category_name: Logistics: appointments, queues, couriers and the physical mechanics
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Consular appointment systems are scraped by bots the instant slots open. The slots are free on the official site and unobtainable there; brokers resell them for hundreds of euros.

details.description: Automated bots scrape appointment systems in real time and capture slots en masse the moment they open, creating artificial scarcity. Reseller platforms openly advertise automated monitoring, instant alerts and auto-booking against VFS Global, TLScontact and BLS systems.
details.energy_note: Competing with software for a place in a queue.

details.description: TURSAB president Firuz Baglikaya said bots take the limited slots the moment the system opens, and appointments then sell for EUR 300-500, reaching EUR 1,000 in urgent cases. A visa services director told NTV some agents demand EUR 500-1,000, 'sometimes even as much as 3,000 euros'.
details.money_note: Black-market price for a free appointment.

details.description: VFS Regional Head for the UAE Monaz Billimoria said bots book slots the moment they are released, creating a 'false or forced limitation', with slots then sold outside at high prices when they are actually free on the VFS website.
details.energy_note: The provider confirms the market exists and cannot stop it.

details.aspect: The countermeasures, and their side effects
details.description: VFS deployed virtual keyboards, IP address restrictions, VPN blocking and a digital waiting room. VPN blocking is a particular problem for Iranians, who routinely need a VPN to reach blocked sites at all - the anti-bot measure locks out the legitimate user.
details.energy_note: Defended against, as a side effect of being Iranian.

details.description: Germany introduced a waiting-list system for short-stay Schengen applications on 18 March 2024, assigning appointments in the order applicants join, which the embassy says stops providers reserving slots in bulk.
details.energy_note: A fix that works, adopted by one country.

details.description: A viral protest movement over chronic appointment shortages, bot scalping, add-on fees, delayed passport returns and aggressive upselling of premium lounge services.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the official denial that helps nobody
details.description: Belgium's ambassador to Turkey said its system does not allow bots, urged applicants to use only VFS, and said unofficial agencies cannot get earlier access - 'This is wasted money.' Applicants who cannot find a slot are left choosing between an official channel with no availability and a broker officially described as a scam.
details.energy_note: Told the only route that works does not work.

details.aspect: The embassy sets the number, not the contractor
details.description: Embassies and consulates, not VFS, control how many appointments exist. The scarcity is a policy choice upstream of the company everyone blames.

There are no Schengen slots in Ankara for eleven weeks. A number circulating in a Telegram group offers an appointment in nine days for EUR 450, payable in advance to a Turkish account. Omid pays. The appointment is real. He never learns who the broker was or where the slot came from.
details.energy_note: Paying a stranger for something that is officially free.

issues.title: Iran's only consular presence in the US is a pass-through
issues.category_name: Logistics: appointments, queues, couriers and the physical mechanics
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: There has been no Iranian embassy in the United States since 1980. The Interests Section, hosted inside the Pakistani embassy, is the only body authorised to provide Iranian consular services - and it decides almost nothing.

details.description: Iran severed relations with the US on 7 April 1980 after the revolution and the hostage crisis. Under the 1981 Algiers Accords each country named a third country as protecting power; Pakistan represents Iranian interests in the US.
details.source_name: Interests Section of Iran in the United States

details.aspect: It is a post box, not an authority
details.description: The Interests Section functions as a pass-through for most document requests, meaning it has limited ability to resolve anything locally. Applications are forwarded to Iran for the actual decision.
details.energy_note: Nobody you can reach has the power to help you.

details.description: Processing at the Interests Section alone takes 4-12 weeks, after which the file goes to Iran for final approval and printing. Total turnaround is typically 6-14 weeks.
details.time_note: Six to fourteen weeks, one document.

details.description: The Interests Section does not accept walk-in applicants for most services. Appointments, where offered at all, must be scheduled in advance - for a single office serving an entire country.
details.energy_note: One office. One country. No door.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - address it to the right tenant
details.description: Guidance warns applicants to address materials to the 'Iranian Interests Section' and NOT to the Pakistani Embassy, despite it being the same building - and to use a trackable courier and keep copies of everything.
details.energy_note: Your life documents, in the post, to the correct sub-tenant.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - even the address is contested
details.description: Published addresses conflict: older references give 2209 Wisconsin Ave NW, current ones 1250 23rd Street NW. The section operated on Wisconsin Avenue from 1981 to 2015 before moving into the Pakistani embassy building - so out-of-date guidance sends documents to a building that has not handled them for a decade.
details.energy_note: Posting your only passport to an address that may be wrong.
details.source_name: Interests Section of Iran in the United States

details.description: Renewal now begins with registration on Iran's Mikhak portal (mikhak.mfa.gov.ir) before any paper is sent - an Iranian government system that must be reached, and made to work, from abroad.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the scale of who depends on it
details.description: In 2003 the Interests Section reported holding passport records for roughly 900,000 Iranians resident in the United States, many of them US-born.
details.source_name: Interests Section of Iran in the United States

issues.title: You must surrender your only passport to renew it
issues.category_name: Logistics: appointments, queues, couriers and the physical mechanics
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Renewal requires submitting the existing Iranian passport. For six to fourteen weeks the applicant holds no Iranian travel document at all - and, if their status abroad depends on it, no way to prove anything.

details.description: The previous Iranian passport must be submitted with the application. If lost or stolen, a police report or notarised statement is required instead.
Six to fourteen weeks with no passport means no international travel, no flight booking, and in many countries no accepted primary identity document.
details.time_note: A window in which you cannot leave or prove who you are.
details.energy_note: Grounded by paperwork, not by law.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - it collides with residence permits
details.description: Many residence permits are physically endorsed in, or linked to, the passport. A renewal that overlaps a permit renewal, a job start date or a re-entry can unpick a lawful status that took years to obtain.
details.money_note: Legal advice, missed start dates, emergency travel documents.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - and a family cannot stagger it
details.description: A family renewing together either sends all passports at once and freezes everyone, or staggers them across six months and freezes someone continuously.
details.energy_note: No arrangement in which everyone can travel.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the fourteen weeks with no passport
details.description: Omid posts his Iranian passport to Washington in February for renewal. His Canadian work permit renewal is due in April and requires a valid passport. He discovers this in March. The Interests Section cannot expedite and cannot return the document mid-process.
details.energy_note: Two deadlines, one document, no way to be in both places.

issues.title: The arrival catch-22
issues.category_name: Logistics: appointments, queues, couriers and the physical mechanics
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by any immigrant regardless of origin
issues.summary: A bank account needs an address. A tenancy needs a bank account and a payslip. A job needs a bank account and a phone number. A phone contract needs an address and a credit check. Every door requires a key kept behind another door.

details.description: Address, bank account, phone number, tax number and proof of income are mutually prerequisite in most destination countries. The loop is broken by whichever institution will bend first.
details.energy_note: Competent, employed, and unable to open a door.

details.description: Breaking the loop usually means paying for short-term accommodation at several times the market rent while queuing for everything else.
details.money_note: Weeks of short-let at a premium.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the deposit nobody has yet
details.description: Tenancies commonly want first month, last month and a deposit up front - before a salary has been paid, and from money that had to be moved out of Iran informally (see FIN-002).

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the sanctions screen fires on arrival
details.description: The bank that finally opens the account runs the same sanctions screen that closes Iranian accounts elsewhere, so the one institution that broke the loop may also be the one that exits the relationship a year later (FIN-001).

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - no guarantor in the country
details.description: Where a local guarantor is required, an immigrant by definition has none, and commercial guarantor services charge a percentage of annual rent.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - eleven days in an Airbnb
details.description: Omid lands in Toronto on a Tuesday. The bank wants a proof of address; the landlord wants a bank statement and a credit check; the phone company wants an address and a credit check. He spends eleven nights at CAD 140 and signs a lease at 30% above market with six months' rent up front, because it is the only one that does not ask.
details.energy_note: Paying a premium for the privilege of not existing yet.

issues.title: Moving a life, by weight
issues.category_name: Logistics: appointments, queues, couriers and the physical mechanics
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by any immigrant regardless of origin
issues.summary: Everything that is not paperwork has to physically travel, be stored, be sold or be abandoned. For Iranians the shipping route itself is constrained by sanctions and by export limits on the way out.

details.description: Most people emigrate with two checked bags. Everything else is sold, given away, or left in a relative's spare room indefinitely.
details.money_note: Excess baggage charges.
details.energy_note: A life, minus what fits.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - freight from Iran is not routine
details.description: International removals companies serving Iran are limited by sanctions exposure, and shipments route through the UAE or Turkey, adding handling, delay and loss risk.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the export caps apply to the shipment too
details.description: The 24 square metres of carpet, 150g of saffron and 150g of gold jewellery limits are not just hand-luggage rules - they cap what leaves at all (see FIN-005).

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - professional tools do not travel
details.description: Engineers' instruments, medical equipment, studio gear and anything dual-use-adjacent can attract export scrutiny on the way out and import scrutiny on the way in.
Personal libraries, family photographs and documents are the highest-value, lowest-weight cargo and the most commonly abandoned, because they are heavy and cannot be replaced.
details.energy_note: The things worth most are the things left behind.

issues.title: Everything must be done in person, in another city
issues.category_name: Logistics: appointments, queues, couriers and the physical mechanics
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Biometrics, interviews, document collection and medical examinations each require physical attendance at a designated centre, often in another country, each on a date set by someone else.

details.description: A typical application chain needs: biometrics enrolment, a consular interview, an approved-panel medical examination, and passport submission and collection - each a separate visit, each with its own scheduling system.
details.time_note: Elapsed across the chain, not working time.

details.description: Immigration medicals must be done by a specific approved doctor. Where no panel physician operates in Iran or the applicant's city, the medical itself becomes an international trip with an expiry date attached.
details.energy_note: A medical certificate that expires before the visa decides.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - results expire out of sync
details.description: Police certificates, medicals and language tests all have validity windows, and a long security screening can outlast them - so documents must be obtained again, at full cost, purely because the decision took too long.
details.energy_note: Paying twice for the same clean record because the state was slow.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - time off work nobody grants
details.description: Each trip is several days of leave. An employee in Iran explaining repeated absences for foreign embassy appointments is also disclosing an intention to emigrate, to an employer who may act on it.
details.energy_note: The process forces you to tell your boss you are leaving.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the medical that expired first
details.description: Omid's immigration medical is done in March and is valid twelve months. Security screening runs nineteen. He is asked to repeat the medical: CAD 450, a new appointment six weeks out, and the same chest X-ray of the same healthy chest.
details.energy_note: Paying again to re-prove a fact that did not change.

issues.title: Single points of failure in a paper chain
issues.category_name: Logistics: appointments, queues, couriers and the physical mechanics
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: The legalised, translated, stamped original exists in one copy, and it travels by courier between countries that do not have reliable postal relations.

details.description: The MoJ-certified translation stapled to the Farsi original, validated by the MFA and endorsed by an embassy, is a single physical artefact. Reproducing it means repeating the entire chain (DOC-001).
details.energy_note: An irreplaceable object in a padded envelope.

details.description: Major couriers restrict or refuse service to and from Iran under sanctions policies, so documents route through third countries or informal carriers - a traveller who happens to be flying.
details.energy_note: Your degree certificate in a stranger's hand luggage.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the consulate holds the passport
details.description: While an application is pending, the post often holds the passport - so the applicant cannot travel, cannot use it as ID, and cannot start a second application elsewhere in parallel.
details.energy_note: One application at a time, enforced physically.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the power of attorney chain
details.description: A man who cannot return to Iran needs a relative to act for him, which needs a power of attorney, which must itself be legalised through the same chain in the other direction before anything can begin.
details.energy_note: A queue that must be completed before you may join the queue.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - and the rules change mid-chain
details.description: Requirements are commonly updated while a file is in transit, so a document legalised correctly in March is rejected in June under a format nobody announced.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the envelope that did not arrive
details.description: Omid's legalised degree set - Farsi original, certified translation, MoJ and MFA stamps - is couriered from Tehran via Istanbul by a family friend flying to Toronto. The friend's connection is cancelled and the bag is checked through to Montreal. It arrives eleven days later. It could have taken four months to replace.
details.energy_note: Your entire education in a stranger's checked luggage.

issues.title: One person, many spellings
issues.category_name: Names: transliteration, misspelling and identity mismatch
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Persian has no single Latin transliteration, so the same name is spelled differently on the passport, the degree, the bank record and the visa. Every mismatch reads to a system as a possible different person.

details.description: Mohammad / Mohammed / Muhammad / Mohamad. Hosseini / Husseini / Hoseini / Hossaini. Reza / Rida. Gholam / Gholam / Qolam. None is a misspelling; they are different romanisations of the same Persian.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the degree does not match the passport
details.description: A degree certificate translated in 2009 and a passport issued in 2016 can carry different spellings, and the credential evaluator treats them as documents about two people.
details.money_note: Re-translation, affidavit, re-legalisation.

details.description: The standard fix is a sworn affidavit that the two names denote the same person - which must itself be notarised, sometimes legalised, and then accepted at the discretion of whoever reads it.
details.energy_note: A legal document asserting that you are yourself.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the airline will not board you
details.description: Airline systems require the ticket to match the travel document. A booking made with the spelling on the old passport, or by an employer's travel desk working from an email signature, can mean denied boarding at the gate with a non-refundable fare.
details.money_note: Change fee or a new one-way fare at the counter.
details.energy_note: Standing at the gate, correctly documented, not travelling.

details.description: Iranian documents often present the family name first. Western forms assume given name first. The result is a person filed under their own first name as a surname, permanently, across an institution.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the father's name has nowhere to go
details.description: Iranian identity documents foreground the father's name. Most Western forms have no field for it, so it lands in the middle-name box on some records and nowhere on others - producing a mismatch generated by the form design itself.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the field is too short
details.description: Legacy systems truncate. A long name is silently cut at 20 or 25 characters in a payroll, insurance or health system, and the truncated version becomes the official one that every later check is run against.
details.energy_note: Your name, as much of it as fitted.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - diacritics eaten by the system
details.description: Where a name has been transliterated with accents or apostrophes - Sa'idi, Ta'ati - systems strip, replace or reject them inconsistently, producing yet another variant.

Omid's ticket, booked by his employer's travel desk from his email signature, reads OMID HOSSEINI. His passport reads HOSEINI. At the gate the agent will not board him. The correction is a name-change fee plus a fare difference: CAD 780, and the meeting in Munich happens without him.
details.energy_note: One letter, one flight, one client.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the degree that belonged to someone else
details.description: WES receives Omid's MSc transcript spelled MOHAMMADI and his passport spelled MOHAMADI. The file goes on hold pending clarification. He obtains a one-and-the-same-person affidavit, notarised and legalised - USD 310 and nine weeks - to establish that he is himself.

issues.title: The spelling someone else chose, permanently
issues.category_name: Names: transliteration, misspelling and identity mismatch
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: A clerk types the name wrong once, and the error propagates. Later systems are populated from the earlier record, so the original typo becomes the authoritative version and correcting it means correcting everything downstream.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the typo on the residence permit
details.description: A misspelling on an immigration document is not a cosmetic problem: the document is the identity. Every subsequent record is created from it, so the error replicates into tax, health, banking and employment.
details.energy_note: Living under a spelling you never chose.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - correcting it is treated as suspicious
details.description: Requesting a correction generates a change-of-name event in systems designed to flag exactly that - so fixing a clerk's typo can trigger the fraud checks that the typo itself never did.
details.energy_note: Punished for asking them to fix their mistake.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the credit file splits in two
details.description: Two spellings produce two thin credit files instead of one good one. The applicant appears to have no history, is refused, and cannot see why.
details.money_note: Higher rates, refused products, required deposits.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the credit file merges with a stranger
details.description: The opposite failure: fuzzy matching attaches another person's accounts or defaults to your file because the names are close enough. The burden of disproving someone else's debt falls on you.
details.energy_note: Refused a mortgage over a stranger's arrears.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the medical record that is not yours
details.description: Health systems match on name and date of birth. A split record means a missing history; a merged record means someone else's allergies, results and medications attached to your file.
details.energy_note: A clinical risk created by a spelling.

details.description: Tax authorities match name against the number. A mismatch rejects the filing, which can cascade into penalties, withheld refunds and a compliance record that later immigration applications ask about.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the background check comes back empty
details.description: A police or employment background check run against a misspelled name returns 'no record found', which is read not as clean but as unverifiable - and an unverifiable applicant is a rejected applicant.
details.energy_note: A clean record that cannot be found is worse than a bad one.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the child's surname does not match the parent's
details.description: Where a child's document was issued with a different romanisation from the parent's, proof of the relationship is questioned - at a school, a hospital, a border, or in a family reunification application.
details.energy_note: Asked to prove your own child is yours.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - two credit files, no credit
details.description: Omid's bank has him as OMID HOSEINI; his employer's payroll reports OMID HOSSEINI to the credit bureau. After three years of perfect payments he applies for a car loan and is told he has insufficient credit history. Both files are eighteen months thin. Neither is wrong.
details.money_note: Higher rate over the loan term, or refusal.
details.energy_note: Three years of good behaviour, split in half.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the allergy that was not his
details.description: A hospital matches Omid to an existing record for an OMID HOSSEINI with the same birth year. The chart lists a penicillin allergy he does not have and omits the beta blocker he does take. He notices because a nurse reads it back to him. Nobody can tell him how long the records have been merged.
details.energy_note: A clinical near-miss produced by a spelling.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - proving his daughter is his
details.description: Omid's daughter is registered in Canada as SARA HOSSEINI. His own permit says HOSEINI. At a border crossing returning from Buffalo, an officer asks him to step aside and establish the relationship. He has no long-form birth certificate with him. It takes ninety minutes and his daughter cries.
details.energy_note: Asked to prove your child is yours, in front of her.

issues.title: The name as a flag
issues.category_name: Names: transliteration, misspelling and identity mismatch
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Beyond mismatch, the name itself is a signal. It triggers sanctions screening false positives, changes callback rates on job applications, and marks the holder before any conversation happens.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - fuzzy matching against a sanctions list
details.description: Screening systems match approximately. A common Persian name can collide with a listed individual, dropping an ordinary transaction into manual review where the customer must prove they are not someone else.
details.energy_note: Proving a negative about a stranger who shares your name.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the Apple Store heard the language, not the name
details.description: In 2012 an Apple employee refused a sale after overhearing Farsi. The trigger does not even need to be written down - speaking is enough (see DIS-003).

Many people apply under a shortened or Anglicised first name. Where the callback rate improves, that improvement is itself the evidence - and the cost is borne silently by the person who edited their own name to get an interview.
details.money_note: Foregone earnings where it does not work - illustrative.
details.energy_note: Editing your name to be employable.

details.description: Being addressed by the wrong name for an hour, or watching an interviewer decide not to attempt it, is a small thing that happens in every professional interaction for a lifetime.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the email address gives it away
details.description: Even where a CV is anonymised, the email address, the university and the country of the phone number restore the signal.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the CV that got callbacks
details.description: After eleven months and about ninety applications, Omid changes the name on his CV to 'Ohm Hoseini' and his email to a first-initial address. He gets three callbacks in five weeks. He does not tell anyone he did this, including his sister.
details.energy_note: The experiment works, and that is the worst part.

issues.title: Denied something you were entitled to, by mistake
issues.category_name: Discretion, clerical error and the agent who got it wrong
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by any immigrant regardless of origin
issues.summary: Eligibility is decided at a counter by a person who may not know the rule. A wrong refusal is not recorded as a refusal - it is recorded as nothing - and the applicant simply does not have the thing they were entitled to.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - Ontario health coverage refused on a waiting period that no longer exists
details.description: Ontario eliminated the three-month OHIP wait for most people in 2020, so coverage is immediate for eligible applicants. A denial based on a 'waiting period' in Ontario is therefore likely to be a clerk error - but the applicant leaves uninsured either way.
details.money_note: Uninsured medical costs during the gap.
details.energy_note: Uninsured because of a rule that was abolished years ago.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the rule is not published, so the clerk invents one
details.description: Ontario does not publish explicit requirements for people on maintained status and instead tells them to contact ServiceOntario to determine eligibility - meaning front-line staff work without clear published rules, which is a recognised source of wrongful refusals.
details.energy_note: No rule to point at, so no way to be right.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the service that exists but is not online
details.description: In Quebec, extending RAMQ coverage on maintained status may be possible but is not offered online - it has to be arranged by telephone. A clerk unfamiliar with it refuses outright, and the applicant has no way to know the option existed.
details.energy_note: Refused a thing you were never told existed.

details.description: Children under 18, recognised refugees and citizens of ten bilateral-agreement countries are exempt from the Quebec waiting period. Each exemption is a rule a busy counter may not apply.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the clock starts when they say it starts
details.description: RAMQ eligibility runs from the registration date provided all documents are submitted; a missing document pushes the start date back. A document wrongly deemed missing costs months of coverage retroactively.
details.energy_note: Backdated exclusion for a document you did provide.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - no reimbursement for the gap
details.description: RAMQ does not reimburse care received before the eligibility start date. If the refusal was wrong and is later corrected, the medical bills incurred meanwhile are still yours.
details.energy_note: Corrected, and still bankrupt.

details.description: The advice that works: get the refusal in writing with the specific reason, escalate past the counter, and file a written review with new evidence under the relevant health insurance act. All of which requires knowing you were wrongly refused in the first place.
details.energy_note: Remedy available only to those who already know the rule.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - uninsured for five months by mistake
details.description: Omid lands in Ontario in 2023 on a work permit. The ServiceOntario clerk tells him there is a three-month wait. There has not been one since 2020. He buys private cover for three months, then lets it lapse, then waits two more months before a colleague tells him to go back. In month four he has appendicitis: CAD 11,400.
details.energy_note: A surgery billed to you because of a rule that was abolished.

issues.title: The outcome depends on which officer you get
issues.category_name: Discretion, clerical error and the agent who got it wrong
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Discretionary standards - 'satisfied that', 'reasonable grounds', 'sufficient ties' - mean two identical files decided by two officers produce opposite results, and neither is wrong.

details.description: In 2024 Sweden refused 51.57% of Iranian Schengen applicants while Switzerland approved 90.25%. Same applicant profile, same Schengen rules, opposite odds depending on which consulate takes the file.
details.energy_note: Your future decided by which building had an appointment.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - a visa granted after a year of vetting, revoked in an afternoon
details.description: The State Department granted Shahab Dehghani a student visa after a year of intense vetting. A CBP officer at Boston Logan revoked it the same day he arrived, on the same facts.
details.energy_note: Two arms of one government, opposite conclusions, no appeal.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the border officer outranks the visa
details.description: A visa is permission to travel to the border and ask. Entry is a separate discretionary decision made by one officer, on the day, with no realistic appeal from inside the airport.
details.energy_note: Everything you built, subject to one person's shift.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - call centre advice that is wrong and binding
details.description: Applicants act on telephone guidance - about eligibility, documents, timing - that turns out to be wrong. The advice is not recorded, is not binding on the department, and the consequence is entirely the applicant's.
details.energy_note: Following the instructions and being penalised for it.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the document that is valid until it is not accepted
details.description: A counter refuses a document that meets the published requirement - wrong translator, wrong stamp, wrong colour of certification - and the applicant cannot escalate past the person in front of them.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - no written reasons, so no appeal
details.description: Where reasons are not given - ATAS refusals, UK visitor refusals, SSSS selection, bank closures - there is no stated ground to rebut, so the procedural right to challenge is formally intact and practically empty.
details.energy_note: An appeal against nothing in particular.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - you find out too late to fix it
details.description: Errors commonly surface after the deadline they affected - a coverage gap discovered at a hospital, a permit error found at a renewal, a name error found at a border. By then the remedy is a new application, not a correction.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the burden of proving the error is yours
details.description: Systems presume their own record is correct. Establishing that an official got it wrong requires documents the applicant may not have been given, about a conversation that was not recorded, with a person who is not identified.
details.energy_note: Disproving an institution from memory.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - and the correction becomes part of your file
details.description: Once corrected, the file contains an inconsistency. Later officers see a record that changed, which is itself a flag - so being the victim of an error leaves a mark that looks like unreliability.
details.energy_note: Their mistake, on your permanent record.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the officer who had a different view
details.description: Omid and his classmate file identical study permit extensions two days apart, same school, same funds, same documents. Hers is approved in nineteen days. His is refused for insufficient proof of funds. They compare the packets line by line and cannot find a difference.
details.energy_note: Two identical files, two answers, no explanation for either.

issues.title: Nobody is accountable for the delay
issues.category_name: Discretion, clerical error and the agent who got it wrong
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Where a decision simply does not arrive, there is no decision to appeal, no service standard that binds, and no official who owns the file.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the call centre can read the screen and nothing else
details.description: An applicant stuck in background check since January 2024 asked whether phoning helps. Agents can report the status; they cannot expedite or escalate.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - not even Congress can move it
details.description: US administrative processing is framed as a national security matter, so universities and members of Congress cannot influence speed or outcome, and once begun it cannot be stopped.
details.energy_note: No lever exists, at any level.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - suing to get an answer, not a yes
details.description: The remedy is mandamus: an action to compel a decision, not a favourable one. Paying several thousand dollars to make the state do its job is standard advice, which is itself the measure of the problem.
The one intuitive self-help action - withdraw and reapply cleanly - restarts processing and triggers the same check, so the system punishes initiative.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the referral is invisible unless you pay to look
details.description: Referral to security screening is never announced. The only way to see it is to request GCMS notes - a separate application, with its own fee and its own wait, to discover why you are waiting.
details.energy_note: An application to find out about your application.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the mandamus he had to fund
details.description: At month 31 Omid's lawyer advises a Federal Court mandamus. It costs CAD 7,500, which is most of his savings, and will compel a decision - not an approval. Six weeks after filing, the application is approved. Nobody says the two events are connected and nobody refunds the CAD 7,500.
details.energy_note: Paying to make the state answer, and never being told if it worked.

issues.title: Single-entry visas, and only for the wrong subjects
issues.category_name: Visas, permits and the right to arrive
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
