issues.summary: Multiple-entry US student visas were opened to Iranians in 2010 - but only for social sciences. Students in technical fields get single entry, so leaving the country once ends the visa. And nobody is told which category they are in.

details.description: Multiple-entry student visas were permitted for Iranians from 2010, but only for students of the social sciences. Students in technical and engineering fields are not eligible and receive single-entry visas only.
details.energy_note: Your field of study decides whether you may ever go home.
details.notes: FOUND ONLY IN PERSIAN SOURCES. Not surfaced by English-language search. Worth confirming against a State Department reciprocity schedule, which is where visa validity and entries are actually published.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - you are not told which you qualify for
details.description: Iranian applicants are not told whether they are eligible for a multiple-entry visa. To find out, they must risk the visa they hold, leave the United States, and reapply - discovering the answer only at that point.
details.money_note: A trip abroad plus a fresh application to learn your own status.
details.time_note: And a new administrative processing hold if the answer is no.
details.energy_note: The only way to learn the rule is to gamble everything on it.

details.description: Single entry plus a Visas Mantis hold on re-application means a technical student who leaves for a funeral may not get back for a year, or at all. This is the mechanism behind the 'stop leaving' behaviour in SEC-003.

Persian coverage of the 2025 restrictions lists the exempt groups: green card holders, dual nationals travelling on a non-designated passport, Olympic and World Cup athletes, US government employees, people with proven family ties, and those holding a valid visa issued before the rule took effect.
details.energy_note: Athletes exempted; students not.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - what Persian-language guidance tells applicants to do
details.description: The practical advice given in Persian is the same as the English: during administrative processing nothing can be done unless the consulate requests something, in which case answer fast and completely. Otherwise, follow the case and wait.
details.energy_note: The advice, in every language, is to wait.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the funeral he does not attend
details.description: Omid is a mechanical engineering PhD student in Michigan on a single-entry F-1. His grandmother dies in Isfahan. If he flies home he must reapply in Yerevan, and the last three people in his lab who did that waited eight, eleven and nineteen months. He watches the burial on a video call at 3am and goes to a seminar at nine.
details.energy_note: The single most common sentence in this whole dataset: he did not go.

issues.title: Georgia: visa-free, and refused at the door
issues.category_name: Borders, airports and secondary inspection
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Georgia is one of the few countries Iranians can enter without a visa, which made it a refuge. Since 2021 Iranians have been turned back at Tbilisi airport and the land borders in large numbers, with no reason given and no appeal.

details.description: Since 2021 growing numbers of Iranians have been denied entry at Georgian land and air borders, particularly Tbilisi International, despite valid passports, return tickets, hotel bookings and sufficient funds.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the reason given is a placeholder
details.description: In many documented cases the only explanation offered is the phrase 'other cases envisaged by Georgian legislation', with no meaningful opportunity to appeal.
details.energy_note: A refusal that cites the existence of law, not any law in particular.

details.description: In 2018 Iranians were the largest single group holding temporary Georgian residency - about 7,300 people, 23% of the total - and in the same year made up the largest share, 20%, of the 16,023 foreigners denied entry.
details.energy_note: The largest resident group and the largest refused group, simultaneously.

details.description: A 26-year-old who had studied in Georgia for eight years was not allowed to board his return flight and was given no explanation - despite a valid residence permit, a negative PCR test and full vaccination.
details.energy_note: Barred from returning to the country you live in.

details.description: An Iranian student and fellow students were already seated on a Tbilisi-bound plane when a flight attendant asked them to disembark. One described being pushed out 'like some kind of terrorists'.
details.energy_note: Removed from your seat in front of everyone.

details.description: Travellers refused entry describe crowded detention rooms with phones and passports confiscated; one account describes an Iranian held there two days without food or communication.
details.energy_note: Detained on arrival in the country that needed no visa.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - 200 at once, with documents in order
details.description: In December 2018 Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Bahram Qassemi said Georgia had denied entry to up to 200 Iranian citizens whose documents were in order.

details.aspect: How it became a refuge in the first place
details.description: Georgia simplified travel rules for Iranians in 2010 and Iranian tourism and investment surged, some arriving for political reasons to escape the Iranian government. The tightening is linked to Iran's deteriorating relations with Georgia's Western partners and Georgia's own immigration crackdown.
details.energy_note: The door that opened, then closed on the people who walked through it.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - and now deportation from inside
details.description: In July 2026 Iranians protested outside Georgia's parliament over Iman Asghari, 37, detained by migration authorities in May and allegedly refused passport renewal by the Iranian embassy - facing deportation to a country his family fears will persecute him.
details.energy_note: Undocumented by one state, deportable by the other.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the flat in Tbilisi he cannot reach
details.description: Reza rents a flat in Tbilisi and registers a small software company there, because Georgia needs no visa. In 2023 he flies back from a client meeting in Yerevan and is refused entry at Tbilisi airport under 'other cases envisaged by Georgian legislation'. His laptop, company documents and cat are in the flat.
details.energy_note: Locked out of a life you may not re-enter to pack up.

issues.title: The Netherlands barred Iranians from whole degree programmes
issues.category_name: Education, credentials and academic recognition
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: From July 2008 Dutch policy forbade Iranian nationals - including Dutch citizens of Iranian descent holding no Iranian passport - from nine degree programmes and several research facilities. A court struck it down in 2010 as discrimination.

details.description: From July 2008 the Dutch government forbade Iranians from courses related to nuclear technology. The foreign ministry said it was forbidden 'to grant Iranian nationals access to special training or teaching that could contribute to nuclear proliferation activities in Iran'.
Even Dutch citizens of Iranian descent who held no Iranian passport were barred from nine degree programmes. Nationality of origin, not current citizenship, was the operative test.
details.energy_note: A Dutch citizen, excluded from a Dutch university, for ancestry.
details.source_name: Library of Congress Global Legal Monitor

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the buildings as well as the courses
details.description: The policy barred Iranians from an experimental reactor at the Nuclear Research and Consultancy Group in Petten, from URENCO, from the Borssele reactor and from a test reactor at Delft University of Technology.
details.energy_note: Physically excluded from buildings on your own campus.

details.aspect: The stated justification, and the real history
details.description: The government said it was implementing UN Security Council Resolution 1737. The Netherlands was especially sensitive because A.Q. Khan, who helped build Pakistan's bomb, gathered information while working at the Dutch URENCO enrichment plant in the 1970s.
details.energy_note: Paying for a security failure that happened before you were born.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - they sued, and they won
details.description: Iranian students and scientists demonstrated at the University of Amsterdam on 1 September 2008 and sued, arguing the ban breached Article 1 of the Dutch Constitution. Plaintiffs included Behnam Taebi, a PhD student at Delft, nuclear physics professor Nasser Kalantar of Groningen, and Delft chemistry student Kawe Bitaraf.
details.energy_note: Named people, who fought it in their own names.

details.description: A court in The Hague found the policy overly broad and in breach of an international civil rights treaty, holding there was 'no objective and reasonable justification' for targeting Iranian students. The 2010 verdict established that Iranian nationals cannot be excluded from facilities or study programmes on the basis of nationality.
details.energy_note: A court saying plainly that it was discrimination.
details.notes: The single most useful precedent in the dataset: nationality-based exclusion tested in court and defeated.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - and it came back anyway
details.description: Years later, following new EU sanctions regulations, the Dutch Immigration and Naturalisation Service halted processing of visa and residency applications made by Iranian citizens. The worst affected were PhD students and applicants in disciplines considered 'sensitive' - a term never clarified.
details.energy_note: Won in court, and the same thing returned under a different name.

issues.title: Australia: detained forever because Iran will not take you back
issues.category_name: Asylum, legal process and representation
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Iranian nationality and being male
issues.summary: Iran refuses to accept citizens deported against their will. Australia detains refused asylum seekers to facilitate removal. The result is detention with no end, lawful because the detainee could theoretically consent to return.

details.aspect: Iran will not take involuntary returnees
details.description: Foreign minister Mohammad Javad Zarif publicly rejected a proposed repatriation deal with Australia in 2016, saying Iran cannot force anybody to return but accepts citizens who come back voluntarily. The deal would have covered almost 9,000 people.
details.energy_note: Neither country will take you, and one of them has you.

details.description: ASF17 arrived in 2013 and was detained continuously from 2014. He refused to consent to return to Iran or to meet Iranian authorities to obtain a travel document, but was willing to be removed to any other country in the world.

During the litigation he disclosed for the first time that he is bisexual, and that his refusal rested on fear of returning to Iran, where sex between men is illegal and can attract the death penalty.
details.energy_note: Forced to disclose the thing you fled, in open court, to explain why you will not go back.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - 'the capacity to change his mind'
details.description: The High Court distinguished the earlier NZYQ ruling and held his detention lawful, because detention remained for the purpose of facilitating departure. The justices noted he had 'the capacity to change his mind' but chose not to. Unanimous.
details.energy_note: Your own refusal to be persecuted, reclassified as your choice to stay in prison.

details.description: Commentators estimated up to 200 people could remain indefinitely detained as a result, and legislation before parliament would have let the minister apply a blanket ban on nationals of countries that refuse deportees - such as Iran.

In January 2026 the UN Committee against Torture found Australia failed to protect an Iranian asylum seeker from torture and ill-treatment across years of detention, first on Manus Island and later on the mainland. He arrived by boat in 2013 and says he was held about three years in harsh conditions and subjected to serious violence.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - eight years on six-month visas
details.description: A separate group recognised as refugees, unable to return to Iran and with nowhere else to go, were evacuated to Australia for urgent medical care between 2015 and 2018 and remain on short-term bridging visas, reapplying every six months.
details.energy_note: A life renewed in six-month increments.

issues.title: Turkey: the address decides, and the address is closed
issues.category_name: Status, residency and citizenship timelines
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Turkey restricts residence permits by neighbourhood rather than by nationality. Iranians are named among the reasons for the policy, and an application at a closed address is rejected automatically.

details.description: From 1 July 2022 the permitted share of foreigners per neighbourhood was cut from 25% to 20%, closing roughly 1,200 districts to new primary residence permits. If your address is in a closed zone the application is automatically rejected.
details.energy_note: Refused by postcode.

details.description: The policy responded to an influx of migrants into popular regions, with the increase from Iraq and Iran cited alongside Russians. The rule is address-based, but the population it was written about is named.
details.energy_note: Neutral on its face, aimed in its explanation.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - eight Istanbul districts at once
details.description: On 7 October 2022 the Interior Minister closed residence permits in eight Istanbul districts - Kucukcekmece, Basaksehir, Bagcilar, Avcilar, Bahcelievler, Sultangazi, Esenler and Zeytinburnu - with no new foreigner registration allowed.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - rent first, find out after
details.description: Buying or renting property in a closed area remains possible - only the permit is refused. A family can sign a lease and then discover the address disqualifies them from living there lawfully.
details.money_note: A lease that cannot produce a permit.
details.energy_note: Legally housed, unlawfully resident.

details.description: Reporting suggests most districts reopened around June 2026, except Fatih and Esenyurt in Istanbul - while other 2026 guidance claims the opposite, that rules tightened, income verification hardened and restricted neighbourhoods increased. The current picture is genuinely contested.
details.energy_note: Nobody can tell you what the rule is this month.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the lease and the postcode
details.description: Omid and Maryam sign a twelve-month lease in Esenyurt because it is what they can afford. The residence permit application is rejected automatically: the district is closed. They are lawfully renting an address at which they may not lawfully reside.
details.money_note: Deposit and break fee.

issues.title: UAE: residency cancelled while you were abroad
issues.category_name: Status, residency and citizenship timelines
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: In 2026 Iranian residents of the UAE - including ten-year golden visa holders - found their residency revoked while they were outside the country, with no right of return and their property, accounts and children's schooling attached to the Emirates ID they no longer had.

details.description: Iranian residents found their visas had been revoked before returning to the UAE, preventing re-entry. In multiple cases non-Iranian family members were still allowed to return while the Iranian national was denied.
details.energy_note: Your family flies home; you do not.

details.description: Holders of ten-year investment-linked 'golden visas' reported cancellation while abroad. If accurate this is the first reported mass cancellation of golden visas in the programme's history.
details.energy_note: The visa you bought for permanence, revoked in your absence.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - everything is tied to the Emirates ID
details.description: Lawyers warn property ownership, bank accounts and children's school places are affected, because most such contracts require a valid Emirates ID. A cancelled resident normally has 30 days to exit or amend status after re-entry - but if the visa is voided while they are outside, there is no right to return at all.
details.money_note: Property and accounts inaccessible.
details.energy_note: One document, and the whole life detaches from it.

details.description: Individuals whose residencies were revoked are reported as being returned to Iran via Afghanistan - transferred to Herat, then crossing by land.
details.energy_note: Sent home the long way, overland, through a third war.

details.description: At least five Iranian schools in the UAE were closed, with student records returned to families.
details.energy_note: Your child's school hands back the file.

details.description: Iran's judiciary said it had revoked the residency permits of 1,200 UAE citizens living in Iran and ordered them to leave within a week. Ordinary people on both sides became the instrument.

details.aspect: The banking precedent was already there
details.description: UAE banks had curbed services for Iranians well before this, with individual salary accounts coming under close scrutiny - so the financial exclusion predates the visa cancellations (see FIN-001).

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the school that returns the file
details.description: Reza's cousin has lived in Dubai for nine years. Her residency is cancelled while she is at a wedding in Istanbul. Her two children's school places lapse with the Emirates ID. The school couriers their records to Istanbul with a compliments slip.
details.energy_note: A family dismantled by an administrative status change.

issues.title: Japan: the visa waiver that was cancelled underneath them
issues.category_name: Visas, permits and the right to arrive
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Iranian nationality and being male
issues.summary: Japan and Iran had mutual visa-free travel. Tens of thousands of young Iranian men came to work after the Iran-Iraq war; Japan cancelled the waiver in 1992 and the population collapsed. The clearest historical case of a door opening and shutting on one cohort.

details.description: A mutual visa waiver dating to 1974 let citizens of either country visit the other without a visa. Migration increased notably from 1989.

After the Iran-Iraq war ended in 1988, many young Iranian men returning from the battlefields could not find work in Iran. Nearly 50,000 entered Japan in 1991, most as tourists permitted three months, and almost all went straight into small factories and service work that young Japanese avoided.
details.energy_note: Demobilised at 22 with no job and an open border.

details.description: With little Japanese and no established community to guide them, workers used Yoyogi and Ueno parks in central Tokyo to exchange news about work and housing. Thousands gathered at weekends; a 1993 report described Yoyogi as resembling 'a Middle Eastern bazaar'.
details.energy_note: A community improvised in a public park because there was nowhere else.

details.description: Unlike Chinese or Korean migrants, Iranians were easily recognised as foreigners, which made foreign labour a visible reality for Japanese society - and made them the face of it.
details.energy_note: Singled out for not blending in.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the numbers, and the cancellation
details.description: Illegal Iranian residents went from 764 in 1990 to 10,915 in 1991 to 40,001 in 1992. The waiver was cancelled in spring 1992 as overstays passed 40,000; with help from Tehran's embassy the number fell by more than 7,000 between May and November. By 2001 it was about 4,300.
details.energy_note: A population of 40,000 legislated down to 4,000.

details.aspect: The minority that defined the majority
details.description: A small minority turned to selling fake phone cards or drugs in the parks, and that became the focus of most press coverage - the standard mechanism by which a whole migrant cohort acquires a reputation.
details.energy_note: Judged by the worst of you, reported by the loudest.

issues.title: The bail you cannot post because your family is in Iran
issues.category_name: Discretion, clerical error and the agent who got it wrong
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Iranian nationality and being male
issues.summary: Bond decisions turn on ties to the country - family, length of residence, employment. A recently-arrived student with all his relatives in Iran scores zero on every limb, so detention continues for having emigrated recently.

details.description: Immigration judges weigh a fixed address in the US, length of residence, family ties, employment history, record of court appearance, criminal record and manner of entry - all to decide danger and flight risk.

The BIA upheld denial of bond where the respondent had no family, employment or community ties and no probable path to lawful status. He had only recently arrived, and the record contained no evidence of family ties, employment history, community ties or court-appearance record in the United States.
details.energy_note: The fact pattern of every new arrival, treated as a reason to detain.
details.notes: This is the legal anchor for the 'my parents are in Iran so I cannot get out' problem. Absence of family here is the stated ground.

details.description: Immigration bond does NOT legally require a US-citizen relative to post it - anyone can pay, including friends or a bond agent. The obstacle is the discretionary flight-risk finding and the amount, not a bar on who may pay.
details.energy_note: Worth knowing: the rule people believe is not the rule.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - no criminal record is not enough
details.description: Practitioners report flight-risk findings based on adverse credibility, refusal to sign documents, and lack of close relatives in the US who are citizens - with no criminal history at all.
details.energy_note: Clean record, still detained, for who is not standing behind you.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - faulted for not having character references
details.description: A Kentucky investigation found judges denying bond or setting unpayable amounts, citing short residence. In one case a judge acknowledged no criminal history but faulted the person for not providing letters attesting to character in the community they had only just joined.
details.energy_note: Asked for character references from a community you arrived in last month.

details.description: The statutory minimum is USD 1,500, but judges routinely set 5,000, 10,000 or 15,000, and cases exist well over 20,000 - payable in full to ICE by cashier's check, from a person whose money is in a country with no banking link.
details.energy_note: A sum that must arrive from a country that cannot wire money.

details.description: The workaround is non-family community ties: leases, sponsor affidavits, employment letters, school records and letters from respected community figures - all of which take time a detained person does not have.
details.energy_note: Assembling a life's worth of references from a detention phone.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - and in one circuit it is worse
details.description: The Fifth Circuit's interpretation in Buenrostro-Mendez v. Bondi renders traditional equitable considerations - family ties, employment, length of residence - legally irrelevant for those it covers. Which circuit detains you changes what evidence even counts.
details.energy_note: The geography of your arrest decides which arguments exist.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the bond he could not make a case for
details.description: Omid is detained after a status lapse caused by a filing error. At the bond hearing the judge asks who in the United States can speak to his character and ties. He has been in the country fourteen months. His parents are in Tehran. His only referee is a lab manager who has known him since September. Bond is set at USD 15,000.
details.energy_note: Detained for the crime of having arrived recently.

issues.title: Being read as a threat, and starting to read yourself that way
issues.category_name: Psychological and social load, and what it costs downstream
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Iranian nationality and being male
issues.summary: Twenty years of screening, secondary inspection and 'are you now or have you ever been' teaches a specific lesson: that you are a risk to be managed. People begin pre-managing themselves, and the self-editing costs more than the screening did.

details.description: Minority stress: chronic, socially-based stressors distinct from ordinary life events, operating through vigilance, expectation of rejection, and concealment. It is an established framework, not a metaphor.

Not posting about politics. Not joining the protest. Not saying where you studied. Not correcting the interviewer's pronunciation. Each is small and rational; together they are a person continuously editing themselves in case they are being assessed.
details.energy_note: Managing an audience that may not be watching, because sometimes it is.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the protest he walked past
details.description: Omid was in Tehran in 2022 and walked past a protest without stopping. In 2026 he still thinks about whether a photograph exists, whether it matters for his file, and whether it counts as evidence for or against him depending who is reading. He has never mentioned it to anyone.
details.energy_note: A memory that is simultaneously your defence and your risk.

details.aspect: The cost is invisible and therefore uncompensated
details.description: None of this appears in any refusal letter or any statistic. It is absorbed privately, which is precisely why it never gets counted as part of the cost of the policy.
'So what brought you to Canada?' Omid has four versions of the answer calibrated to how the room feels. The short one, the technical one, the warm one, and the true one, which he has never used.
details.energy_note: Four rehearsed autobiographies, and none of them yours.

issues.title: The gratitude imperative
issues.category_name: Psychological and social load, and what it costs downstream
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by any immigrant regardless of origin
issues.summary: Host societies expect appreciation, and the expectation is itself a form of control - it makes criticism, grief and ordinary complaint look like ingratitude. Scholars argue the duty does not actually exist.

details.aspect: The argument that there is no such duty
details.description: Buxton and Gibney (Political Studies, 2025) argue no duty of gratitude is owed to the asylum state, because the state-imposed barriers and hardships refugees must endure to reach asylum undermine it. Any gratitude is owed instead to those who helped them evade those restrictions - and resentment is often the more apt response.
details.energy_note: Permission, from a journal, to stop performing.
details.source_name: Must Refugees Be Grateful?, Political Studies

details.aspect: Gratitude as a debt that never clears
details.description: Mimi Nguyen's framing treats gratitude as a social emotion binding refugees to the state in an 'endless cycle of debt repayment'. Refuge is framed as a conditional gift demanding repayment.
details.energy_note: A gift you are still paying for twenty years later.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - told publicly that you owe
details.description: Tucker Carlson claimed in 2020 that Rep. Ilhan Omar, resettled in 1995, still owed duties of gratitude to the US that should shape how she behaves and feels - twenty-five years later, as a sitting member of Congress.
details.energy_note: Elected, and still asked to say thank you.

details.description: Dina Nayeri's The Ungrateful Refugee recounts people who assumed she was grateful, or thought she ought to be. The book exists because the expectation is universal enough to name.
details.source_name: The Ungrateful Refugee, via Buxton & Gibney

details.aspect: The double bind for the competent
details.description: A skilled migrant who arrived by every rule, paid every fee and was refused repeatedly is still expected to speak of the destination as a rescue. Describing it accurately - as a transaction he mostly funded - reads as arrogance.
details.energy_note: Accuracy misheard as ingratitude.

details.description: Someone says 'you must be so happy to be here' and Omid says yes. He is thinking about the twenty-six months, the CAD 7,500, the father he did not bury. He says yes because the alternative is a conversation he will lose.
details.energy_note: Agreeing, because disagreeing costs more than it is worth.

details.aspect: It also lands on the host
details.description: Research on Ukrainian refugees in Poland - 30 refugees and 24 hosts - found hosts experienced gratitude variably, including as a burden producing awkwardness. The expectation damages both sides of the exchange.
details.notes: Useful nuance: this is not simply hosts being cruel.

issues.title: Being counted as a cost
issues.category_name: Psychological and social load, and what it costs downstream
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by any immigrant regardless of origin
issues.summary: Public opinion treats immigrants as a net drain on the welfare state, largely inaccurately. Living inside a story about yourself that the evidence does not support is its own chronic load.

details.description: A key driver of reduced welfare support is the belief that immigrants disproportionately burden welfare systems - accompanied by measurable misperceptions, including overestimating both the number of immigrants and their economic dependence.

details.aspect: What the fiscal evidence actually says
details.description: Fiscal contribution varies: high-skilled immigrants generally contribute positively; low-skilled and humanitarian entrants can pose short-term costs, usually mitigated over time. Public concern often reflects broader cultural anxieties rather than the evidence.
details.energy_note: The skilled migrant is a net contributor, and is resented anyway.

details.description: Nearly 42% of Austrian respondents believe social rights for newcomers should be conditional on citizenship (26.4%) or withheld entirely (15.4%).

details.aspect: Immigration became the lens for welfare itself
details.description: Xu, Davis, Garand and Danielson argue immigration is now the dominant frame through which Americans think about welfare. The effect is asymmetric: people with negative views of immigrants support welfare less where immigrant participation is higher, while for those with positive views it does not reduce support and sometimes slightly increases it.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the taxes he does not mention
details.description: Omid has paid income tax in Ontario for four years, has never claimed a benefit, and waited three months for a family doctor he still does not have. A colleague complains at lunch that immigrants are straining the system. He says nothing, because the arithmetic would sound defensive.
details.energy_note: Holding the receipts and not producing them.

details.description: The welfare-burden story and the gratitude imperative run on the same machinery: one casts you as a taker, the other demands you perform appreciation as the price of staying. They are the same demand from two directions.

issues.title: The intimate market
issues.category_name: Psychological and social load, and what it costs downstream
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Iranian nationality and being male
issues.summary: Dating and partner formation are stratified by ethnicity in measurable ways, and immigration status narrows the field further. The popular version of this claim is stronger than the data - which matters, because the belief does damage independent of the reality.

details.description: OkCupid's response-rate data (2009-2014) and a study of 2.4 million heterosexual interactions on Facebook's 'Are You Interested?' both found Black men, Black women and Asian men received the fewest responses; white men and Asian women the most.
details.notes: IMPORTANT CALIBRATION: Middle Eastern men are NOT typically the lowest-response group in these datasets. The disadvantage is real but smaller than the folk version, and the folk version is itself harmful.

details.aspect: Why the Middle Eastern numbers are weak
details.description: One analysis flags sampling problems: OkCupid skewed young, educated and liberal, probably representing whites better than Middle Easterners, with more assimilated users self-selecting onto the platform specifically to date outside their group.

details.aspect: Stated preference moved; behaviour did not
details.description: Between 2009 and 2014 the share of OkCupid users saying they would date someone with a vocal racial bias fell from 27% to 10% - while actual behaviour barely changed.
details.energy_note: Everyone got better at saying it and nobody changed.

details.description: Users tend to segregate by race, and where a demographic receives fewer swipes the algorithm shows them to fewer people - a feedback loop that turns a modest initial skew into a large practical one.
details.energy_note: A small bias, compounded by software into a wall.

details.aspect: Status insecurity as its own filter
details.description: Independent of ethnicity: a man on a temporary permit who cannot say where he will live in eighteen months, cannot sign a lease or a mortgage, and may be refused re-entry, is a poor prospect for anyone planning a life. The visa does the filtering the prejudice is blamed for.
details.energy_note: Not undesirable - unplannable.

details.description: It comes on the third date, always kindly: so are you staying? Omid explains maintained status, the background check, the possibility of a refusal. He watches her do the arithmetic he has already done. There is no bad behaviour anywhere in the evening.
details.energy_note: Rejected by a spreadsheet nobody wrote down.

details.aspect: The belief does damage on its own
details.description: A man who believes he is categorically unwanted approaches fewer people, invests less, and reads ordinary rejection as confirmation. The folk statistic is more disabling than the real one.
details.notes: Deliberate: the honest reading of the data is also the more useful one. See PSY-009 - part of why this data is poor is that it collapses Iranians into a Middle Eastern bucket they do not belong in.

issues.title: Vulnerability in relationships where status is asymmetric
issues.category_name: Psychological and social load, and what it costs downstream
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by any immigrant regardless of origin
issues.summary: Where one partner's right to remain depends on the other, or on a job the other controls, ordinary relationship conflict acquires immigration consequences. The asymmetry is structural, not a matter of character.

details.description: Dependent and spousal visas tie status to a relationship. Ending the relationship can end the right to remain, which changes what leaving costs and therefore what can be tolerated.
details.energy_note: Unable to leave for reasons that have nothing to do with love.

details.aspect: It is not gender-specific, and it is not symmetrical
details.description: It applies to whoever holds the dependent status. In practice that is more often the woman, but an Iranian man on a spousal permit is in exactly the same position and has fewer services aimed at him.

A person with eighteen months of status remaining is choosing a partner against a deadline, which is a bad condition for choosing anything. Both the rushing and the settling are produced by the permit.
details.energy_note: Choosing a life against a countdown.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the engagement that was really a deadline
details.description: Maryam's permit expires in July. The relationship is eleven months old and fine, not certain. They get engaged in April. Neither of them says the word 'permit' during the conversation, and both of them are thinking about it.
details.energy_note: A decision made by a date stamp.

details.description: Where abuse occurs, the dependent partner may reasonably believe that reporting risks their status, their children's schooling and their right to stay - so the structural incentive runs toward silence.
details.notes: Well recognised in domestic violence and immigration practice; most jurisdictions have some provision for it. Layer-5 target: the specific protections and their real-world uptake.

details.aspect: The protection exists and it is slow
details.description: US VAWA self-petition lets an abused spouse of a citizen or permanent resident apply for status without the abuser's knowledge, consent or involvement. USCIS does not notify third parties and the petitioner can designate a safe address. No police report is required.
details.energy_note: The remedy is real, which matters.
details.notes: ANSWERS PSY-005-005.

details.aspect: Three and a half to four years
details.description: 2026 USCIS data puts I-360 processing at roughly 41.5-46.5 months for 80% of cases, with adjustment of status adding another 8-24 months. Work authorisation is what lets a survivor support herself without the abuser - and it is years away.
details.energy_note: A way out that takes four years to open.
details.source_name: USCIS processing data via practitioner analysis

details.description: Qualifying abuse includes physical and sexual abuse, threats of violence, verbal degradation, emotional abuse, isolation, intimidation, ECONOMIC ABUSE, and threats to take the children or have the victim deported - which is the specific threat that immigration status makes credible.
details.energy_note: The threat to have you deported is itself listed as the abuse.

details.aspect: Denied for reasons unrelated to the abuse
details.description: One practitioner analysis reports 18% of 2024 VAWA petitions denied on grounds unconnected to the abuse claim - prior immigration issues, certain convictions, unlawful presence triggering three- or ten-year bars, final removal orders. Waivers exist and add complexity.
details.energy_note: Surviving it, and still failing on a technicality from years earlier.

details.aspect: And the category queue still applies
details.description: Self-petitioners who are immediate relatives of US citizens can adjust on approval; spouses and children of permanent residents must still wait for a visa number in their category.

issues.title: The bandwidth tax
issues.category_name: Psychological and social load, and what it costs downstream
issues.applies_to_note: Faced by any immigrant regardless of origin
issues.summary: Scarcity of any kind consumes the mental capacity normally used for planning, problem-solving and self-control. This is measured, it is large, and it is the honest mechanism behind 'I used to have ideas'.

details.description: Mullainathan and Shafir's experiments showed scarcity taxes the same person's cognitive performance, reducing effective intelligence and self-control by roughly a full standard deviation - making people appear less capable than they are.
details.energy_note: Not less able. Occupied.
details.source_name: Mani et al., Poverty impedes cognitive function, Science 341 (2013)

details.description: Scarcity produces intense focus on the pressing need at the expense of everything peripheral. Time-scarce people miss medical appointments; money-scarce people miss bill payments - not from indifference but because those things fall outside the tunnel.
details.energy_note: The dentist appointment was never a decision. It was invisible.

details.aspect: It is situational, and it lifts
details.description: Bandwidth is not permanently damaged. Farmers' cognitive capacity was restored as soon as crop payments arrived. When the pressure lifts, the capacity returns.
details.energy_note: The single most hopeful finding in this dataset.
details.notes: Important for the game: this is reversible, and saying so is accurate.

details.aspect: Immigration is a scarcity of the relevant kind
details.description: An open application with no decision date is scarcity of certainty. It occupies bandwidth continuously, for years, in exactly the way the research describes - and unlike money, no payment arrives to release it.

Social scarcity behaves the same way. In an Einstein Aging Study sample, higher daily loneliness predicted worse same-day processing speed and memory binding, and worse performance the next day - holding even after controlling for momentary depressed mood.
details.energy_note: The isolation is not just painful. It is measurably expensive.
details.notes: CALIBRATION: this literature is dominated by ageing and dementia-risk framing and causality runs both ways. The momentary within-person findings support the bandwidth reading; the longitudinal ones are weaker.

details.aspect: Which is the defensible version of the 'no ideas' claim
details.description: There is no evidence for a direct line from sexual or romantic dissatisfaction to fewer business ideas. There is good evidence that unresolved preoccupation of any kind - money, status, isolation, an open file - consumes the same bandwidth that side projects, risk-taking and original thinking run on.
details.energy_note: The ideas did not leave. The capacity to hold them did.
details.notes: Deliberately stated this way. The mechanism is real; the specific causal chain in the popular version is not established.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the side project that never started
details.description: Omid had a design for a modular test rig in 2022. It is still four sketches and a spreadsheet. Every evening for three years has had a form in it, or a portal check, or a phone call about a form. He is not lazy and he has not lost interest. He has no slack.
details.money_note: Unbuilt - illustrative, not measured.

details.description: The research names the antidote: slack, the buffer that allows decisions without constant trade-offs. Anything that creates certainty - a decision date, permanent status, a stable account - returns capacity directly.
details.energy_note: What actually helps, and it is not resilience.

issues.title: The body keeps the score
issues.category_name: Psychological and social load, and what it costs downstream
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: Chronic discrimination stress shows up physiologically - cardiovascular risk, metabolic and immune dysregulation. The pain and fatigue link is plausible and much less well evidenced than the cardiac one.

details.description: The framework linking chronic social stress to disease: dysregulation across cardiovascular, metabolic, immune, sympathetic and HPA-axis systems - the 'wear and tear' that accumulates through repeated stress exposure. It rises between ages 20 and 60.
details.energy_note: The bill arrives twenty years later, itemised as something else.

details.description: A study of 1,714 migrants in Spain found discrimination and psychological distress predicted cardiovascular risk, with distress mediating the relationship - and the association held with socioeconomic variables controlled.
details.source_name: Perceived Discrimination, Psychological Distress and Cardiovascular Risk in Migrants in Spain

details.aspect: The pain link is weaker than people assume
details.description: Chronic pain and fatigue appear associated with mild HYPOcortisolism - a different HPA pathway from the hypercortisol pattern of acute stress. Standard allostatic load indices may not capture discrimination-related pain well, and pain is underrepresented in this literature.
details.energy_note: The back pain is probably real and is not well proven.
details.notes: HONEST LIMIT. The user's back-pain intuition is biologically plausible and the evidence base is thin. Layer-5 target: the discrimination-pain literature specifically.

details.aspect: The immigrant paradox cuts the other way
details.description: Some research finds allostatic load LOWER in foreign-born people, who reported fewer experiences of discrimination alongside healthier diets and safer neighbourhoods. Migration is not uniformly bad for health, and saying so keeps the rest credible.
details.notes: Included deliberately. A dataset that only points one way is less useful.

details.description: Close relationships affect cardiovascular, immune and neuroendocrine functioning during stress. Passive, physical and verbal support all buffer cardiovascular stress responses - and in lab settings even strangers work.
details.energy_note: Company is not a consolation prize. It is the intervention.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the thing the doctor cannot find
details.description: Omid's shoulder and lower back have hurt since 2023. Two physiotherapists, an X-ray and an MRI find nothing structural. He is told it is probably stress. He agrees, pays CAD 1,100 in physio, and does not mention the application.
details.energy_note: A symptom with no diagnosis and an obvious cause nobody writes down.

details.description: Hassan's brother emigrated to Sweden in 1998 and had a heart attack at 54. The family says it was the cigarettes. It was probably partly the cigarettes.
details.energy_note: Attributed to the visible cause, as it always is.

issues.title: What it costs the career
issues.category_name: Psychological and social load, and what it costs downstream
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Iranian nationality and being male
issues.summary: The downstream effect of everything above: lower risk appetite, fewer moves, less negotiation, no venture. Not because of ability, but because the buffer that permits risk was spent on the process.

details.description: Leaving a job, founding a company or taking a pay cut for a better trajectory all require slack. A permit tied to an employer removes the option entirely; an open application makes any change look like a risk to the file.
details.energy_note: Every career move is also an immigration decision.

details.aspect: You cannot negotiate from a visa
details.description: An employee whose status depends on the employer has materially less bargaining power, and both sides know it. The salary gap compounds across every subsequent offer, which are benchmarked against it.
details.money_note: Cumulative differential over a career - illustrative.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the raise he did not ask for
details.description: Omid has been underpaid by roughly CAD 18,000 for two years. He knows. His PR application names this employer. He decides to ask after it lands, which is what he decided last year.
details.energy_note: Every year the right time to ask is next year.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the company he did not found
details.description: Two colleagues leave to start something and ask Omid to join as the third. Founding requires giving up the employer-tied permit. He says no and stays. The company is acquired four years later.
details.energy_note: The fork in the road, foreclosed by paperwork.

details.aspect: And it is read as a personality
details.description: From outside, all of this looks like caution, or lack of ambition, or not being a self-starter. It is a rational response to conditions nobody in the room can see.
details.energy_note: Your constraints, mistaken for your character.

issues.title: Depicted as something you are not
issues.category_name: Psychological and social load, and what it costs downstream
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Iranian nationality and being male
issues.summary: Iranians are Persian, not Arab - Farsi is Indo-European, Arabic is Semitic - and Western media has spent forty years collapsing the distinction and casting Iranian men specifically as zealots and domestic tyrants. People arrive pre-characterised by films they have never seen.

details.description: Evelyn Alsultany: 'It is commonly assumed that Iranians and Pakistanis are Arab and that all Arabs are Muslim and all Muslims Arab.' Farsi belongs to the Indo-European family; Arabic is Semitic. The overgeneralisation erases cultural distinctions and feeds prejudice.
details.energy_note: Judged as a member of a group you are not in.

details.description: The New York Times' Caryn James wrote that it 'exploits the stereotype of the demonic Iranian'. The Los Angeles Times called it 'unbalanced and distorted' for failing to distinguish the Iranian state from the Iranian people. Roger Ebert said it made 'moral and racial assertions that are deeply troubling' and 'does not play fair with its Muslim characters'.
details.source_name: Not Without My Daughter, critical reception

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the academic reading is the point exactly
details.description: A UC Irvine analysis argues Americans took the account not as a memoir of domestic discord but as an authentic representation of Iranian practice - and that the husband's violence is framed in the film as 'the pinnacle of Iranian masculinity'.
details.energy_note: One man's violence, presented as the definition of your gender and nationality at once.

details.description: Reza Aslan has described the film as an 'albatross' for many Iranians in the US, saying it reinforced stereotypes of abusive Iranian men and an oppressive Islamic society. It flopped - and for years was one of the only American films about Iran, which is why it mattered.
details.energy_note: A bad film nobody liked, doing forty years of damage because it was the only one.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - it was not even filmed there
details.description: The film was shot largely in Israel, with Russian extras cast as Iranian citizens in crowd scenes.
details.energy_note: Not one Iranian in the crowd.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - and it kept being shown
details.description: It has been screened in schools and re-aired on television, and was shown in Paris the night before the 1998 USA v Iran World Cup match. When Iranian communities objected, one journalist told them to 'shut up', arguing the film was so unremarkable the grievance was illogical.
details.energy_note: Objecting to it is reframed as your oversensitivity.

details.description: Ajam Media Collective traces the line: Not Without My Daughter's husband turning zealot, 300 casting ancient Persians as the enemies of the West, and Argo collapsing Iranians into a faceless mob - together building a picture of a people stripped of ordinary inner life.
details.energy_note: Three decades of being scenery in someone else's story.
details.source_name: Ajam Media Collective - Reel Bad Iranians

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - the escape hatch, and its price
details.description: Many young Iranian Americans feel caught between two stereotypes - the bearded fanatic and the materialistic gold-wearing 'Persian' - and many choose the second. Maz Jobrani's joke, 'I'm not Iranian, I'm Persian', names it. Some note that 'Persian' is itself a label imposed from outside.
details.energy_note: Escaping one caricature by adopting another.

details.aspect: Better writing does not fix it
details.description: Alsultany warns that 'simplified complex representations' do not challenge stereotypes but affirm them under the guise of cultural sensitivity - reassuring audiences that racial sensitivity is the norm while still presenting Iranians, Arabs and Muslims as national security threats.
details.energy_note: The sympathetic portrayal that leaves the conclusion intact.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the thing his girlfriend's father said
details.description: Maryam's Canadian boyfriend's father is friendly all evening and then says, meaning it warmly, that Omid seems 'very Westernised, not like you'd expect'. It is intended as the highest compliment available. Omid thanks him.
details.energy_note: Praised for the distance between you and what they assumed.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the kindness that reads as strategy
details.description: Omid is careful, soft-spoken and does most of the cooking. A colleague tells him, admiringly, that he is 'not like other Middle Eastern guys'. He has never been a Middle Eastern guy. He is Iranian, and he was raised by a chemistry teacher in Karaj who cried at weddings.
details.energy_note: Your actual personality, received as an exception to a rule about you.

issues.title: The service card runs your life inside Iran, not just the exit
issues.category_name: Military service and the male exit problem
issues.applies_to_note: Requires both Iranian nationality and being male
issues.summary: The military service completion or exemption card is a de facto internal identity document. Without one a man cannot get a passport, cannot get a driver's licence, cannot hold a government job and is 'not hired for high-paying jobs'. Emigration is blocked at the far end of a chain that already blocked everything else.

details.aspect: It is required for a passport, in principle
details.description: Citing the Iranian MFA's Main Office for Consular Services, Landinfo reports that male applicants of conscription age seeking a passport must 'in principle' attach a card showing completion of or exemption from military service, in original and copy.
details.notes: ANSWERS MIL-001-008. The document chain is now sourced to an IRB Response to Information Request, not inference.

details.description: Refusing to serve without an exemption can result in not being granted a driver's licence - so the same status that blocks the passport also blocks ordinary domestic mobility.
details.energy_note: Unable to leave the country, and unable to drive across the city.

details.description: Men who refuse service without an exemption are ineligible for government jobs and, in the IHRDC's phrasing, 'not hired for high-paying jobs'. The penalty is not a fine; it is a permanent ceiling on earnings.
details.energy_note: Priced out of your own economy at nineteen.

details.description: IHRDC notes that failing to serve without an exemption can also result in 'a ban on leaving the country without special permission' - an explicit exit control, separate from simply not being issued a passport.

details.aspect: The card states WHY you were exempted
details.description: When an exemption is obtained the holder is issued a card which lists the reason for the exemption. A medical or psychiatric exemption is therefore written on a document used as routine identification.
details.energy_note: Your diagnosis, printed on your ID, shown to every clerk.

details.aspect: It is used as an identity document
details.description: Landinfo, citing Iran's National Organization for Civil Registration, notes that completion or exemption cards count as valid photo ID in an application package for a new shenasnameh. The US reciprocity schedule describes both cards as 'readily available'.
Among the non-health grounds for exemption is being the only son of the family - which means the exemption available to most men is an accident of sibling order.
Men exempted before 1990 may never have been issued a card explaining the reason - so an older applicant asked abroad to evidence his status may have nothing to produce, through no fault of his own.
details.energy_note: A document that was never issued, demanded thirty years later.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the card he cannot show either way
details.description: Omid's exemption card reads, in Persian, the ground on which he was excused. He needs it for the Canadian file. He also does not want a visa officer reading it. There is no version of the document that says only what he wants it to say.
details.energy_note: The proof you need is also the disclosure you dread.

issues.title: The law is on your side, and companies keep being fined for not knowing it
issues.category_name: Work, licensing, export control and clearance
issues.applies_to_note: Triggered by Iranian nationality, passport or place of birth
issues.summary: DOJ has repeatedly penalised employers who used export control as a reason to hire only US citizens. ITAR's own definition of 'US person' includes permanent residents, asylees and refugees - so most of the exclusions Iranians meet are not merely unnecessary, they are unlawful.

details.aspect: Export control is not a hiring rule
details.description: DOJ's position: the ITAR and the EAR contain no employment or hiring requirements and do not require employers or staffing agencies to limit jobs to US citizens. If a foreign person's job needs access to controlled technical data, the employer obtains a licence for that person.
details.energy_note: The reason you were given does not exist in the regulation.
details.notes: ANSWERS EMP-001-005.

details.aspect: The definition that employers get wrong
details.description: ITAR 120.62 defines 'US person' to include lawful permanent residents under 8 USC 1101(a)(20) AND 'protected individuals' under 8 USC 1324b(a)(3) - which covers asylees and refugees. Restricting an export-controlled role to citizens and green card holders unlawfully excludes asylees and refugees.
details.energy_note: Three categories of lawful worker, excluded by a definition nobody read.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - Clifford Chance US LLP, 2018, USD 132,000
details.description: DOJ found the firm unlawfully restricted staffing by citizenship status, excluding non-US citizens AND DUAL US CITIZENS from document review involving ITAR-controlled data. DOJ attributed it to a misunderstanding of ITAR. Civil penalty: USD 132,000.
details.energy_note: Dual citizens excluded - which is every Iranian-American, because Iran will not let the nationality go.
details.source_name: DOJ IER settlements via National Law Review
details.notes: The dual-citizen element connects directly to STA-002: Iranians cannot renounce, so this exclusion lands on them permanently.

details.description: DOJ found at least 25 job postings requiring applicants to be 'lawful permanent residents and/or US citizens' without valid justification, again from a misunderstanding of ITAR/EAR. Penalty USD 44,626 plus two years of DOJ monitoring.

details.aspect: EXAMPLE - American CyberSystems, and General Motors
details.description: DOJ concluded there was no justification for excluding US nationals, asylees and refugees from a posting, because no authorisation was needed to share controlled items with them. Separately DOJ determined GM's method of running export compliance assessments discriminated against non-US workers, and issued an employer fact sheet alongside the settlement.

details.aspect: The exact postings that are unlawful
details.description: DOJ names them: 'Only U.S. Citizens', 'Only U.S. Citizens or Green Card Holders', or demanding a US birth certificate - even where the role genuinely requires authorisation. The recommended wording is 'U.S. person'.
details.energy_note: If you have seen those words on a posting, you have seen a violation.

details.aspect: Do not merge the export check with the I-9
details.description: DOJ advises against combining an export compliance assessment with the Form I-9 process - a common practice that turns a document check into a citizenship screen.

details.aspect: Settlements are rising, and they are small
details.description: IER reaches dozens of settlements annually, with a small but increasing share tied to EAR/ITAR/DOE compliance. The penalties - USD 44,626, USD 132,000 - are rounding errors for the companies involved, which is why the practice persists.
details.energy_note: A remedy that exists, works, and costs the employer less than complying would have.

details.aspect: SCENARIO - the posting he screenshots and does nothing about
details.description: Omid finds a role he is qualified for. The posting says 'Must be a U.S. Citizen or Green Card Holder'. He is an asylee, which makes him a protected individual and a US person. He screenshots it, looks up how to file with IER, reads that it takes months, and applies somewhere else.
details.energy_note: Holding a valid legal claim and no time to use it.
